Often, in mild,\npleasant weather, for twelve, fifteen, eighteen, and twenty hours on the\nstretch, they were engaged in the boats, steadily pulling, or sailing,\nor paddling after the whales, or for an interlude of sixty or seventy\nminutes calmly awaiting their uprising; though with but small success\nfor their pains.\n\nAt such times, under an abated sun; afloat all day upon smooth, slow\nheaving swells; seated in his boat, light as a birch canoe; and so\nsociably mixing with the soft waves themselves, that like hearth-stone\ncats they purr against the gunwale; these are the times of dreamy\nquietude, when beholding the tranquil beauty and brilliancy of the\nocean\u2019s skin, one forgets the tiger heart that pants beneath it;\nand would not willingly remember, that this velvet paw but conceals a\nremorseless fang.\n\nThese are the times, when in his whale-boat the rover softly feels a\ncertain filial, confident, land-like feeling towards the sea; that he\nregards it as so much flowery earth; and the distant ship revealing\nonly the tops of her masts, seems struggling forward, not through high\nrolling waves, but through the tall grass of a rolling prairie: as when\nthe western emigrants\u2019 horses only show their erected ears, while\ntheir hidden bodies widely wade through the amazing verdure.\n\nThe long-drawn virgin vales; the mild blue hill-sides; as over these\nthere steals the hush, the hum; you almost swear that play-wearied\nchildren lie sleeping in these solitudes, in some glad May-time, when\nthe flowers of the woods are plucked. And all this mixes with your most\nmystic mood; so that fact and fancy, half-way meeting, interpenetrate,\nand form one seamless whole.\n\nNor did such soothing scenes, however temporary, fail of at least as\ntemporary an effect on Ahab. But if these secret golden keys did seem\nto open in him his own secret golden treasuries, yet did his breath upon\nthem prove but tarnishing.\n\nOh, grassy glades! oh, ever vernal endless landscapes in the soul; in\nye,\u2014though long parched by the dead drought of the earthy life,\u2014in\nye, men yet may roll, like young horses in new morning clover; and for\nsome few fleeting moments, feel the cool dew of the life immortal on\nthem. Would to God these blessed calms would last. But the mingled,\nmingling threads of life are woven by warp and woof: calms crossed by\nstorms, a storm for every calm. There is no steady unretracing progress\nin this life; we do not advance through fixed gradations, and at the\nlast one pause:\u2014through infancy\u2019s unconscious spell, boyhood\u2019s\nthoughtless faith, adolescence\u2019 doubt (the common doom), then\nscepticism, then disbelief, resting at last in manhood\u2019s pondering\nrepose of If. But once gone through, we trace the round again; and are\ninfants, boys, and men, and Ifs eternally. Where lies the final harbor,\nwhence we unmoor no more? In what rapt ether sails the world, of which\nthe weariest will never weary? Where is the foundling\u2019s father hidden?\nOur souls are like those orphans whose unwedded mothers die in bearing\nthem: the secret of our paternity lies in their grave, and we must there\nto learn it.\n\nAnd that same day, too, gazing far down from his boat\u2019s side into that\nsame golden sea, Starbuck lowly murmured:\u2014\n\n\u201cLoveliness unfathomable, as ever lover saw in his young bride\u2019s\neye!\u2014Tell me not of thy teeth-tiered sharks, and thy kidnapping\ncannibal ways. Let faith oust fact; let fancy oust memory; I look deep\ndown and do believe.\u201d\n\nAnd Stubb, fish-like, with sparkling scales, leaped up in that same\ngolden light:\u2014\n\n\u201cI am Stubb, and Stubb has his history; but here Stubb takes oaths\nthat he has always been jolly!\u201d\n\n\n\n\n\nCHAPTER 115. The Pequod Meets The Bachelor.\n\nAnd jolly enough were the sights and the sounds that came bearing down\nbefore the wind, some few weeks after Ahab\u2019s harpoon had been welded.\n\nIt was a Nantucket ship, the Bachelor, which had just wedged in her\nlast cask of oil, and bolted down her bursting hatches; and now, in glad\nholiday apparel, was joyously, though somewhat vain-gloriously, sailing\nround among the widely-separated ships on the ground, previous to\npointing her prow for home.\n\nThe three men at her mast-head wore long streamers of narrow red bunting\nat their hats; from the stern, a whale-boat was suspended, bottom down;\nand hanging captive from the bowsprit was seen the long lower jaw of the\nlast whale they had slain. Signals, ensigns, and jacks of all colours\nwere flying from her rigging, on every side. Sideways lashed in each of\nher three basketed tops were two barrels of sperm; above which, in her\ntop-mast cross-trees, you saw slender breakers of the same precious\nfluid; and nailed to her main truck was a brazen lamp.\n\nAs was afterwards learned, the Bachelor had met with the most surprising\nsuccess; all the more wonderful, for that while cruising in the same\nseas numerous other vessels had gone entire months without securing a\nsingle fish. Not only had barrels of beef and bread been given away to\nmake room for the far more valuable sperm, but additional supplemental\ncasks had been bartered for, from the ships she had met; and these\nwere stowed along the deck, and in the captain\u2019s and officers\u2019\nstate-rooms. Even the cabin table itself had been knocked into\nkindling-wood; and the cabin mess dined off the broad head of an\noil-butt, lashed down to the floor for a centrepiece. In the forecastle,\nthe sailors had actually caulked and pitched their chests, and filled\nthem; it was humorously added, that the cook had clapped a head on his\nlargest boiler, and filled it; that the steward had plugged his spare\ncoffee-pot and filled it; that the harpooneers had headed the sockets\nof their irons and filled them; that indeed everything was filled with\nsperm, except the captain\u2019s pantaloons pockets, and those he reserved\nto thrust his hands into, in self-complacent testimony of his entire\nsatisfaction.\n\nAs this glad ship of good luck bore down upon the moody Pequod, the\nbarbarian sound of enormous drums came from her forecastle; and drawing\nstill nearer, a crowd of her men were seen standing round her huge\ntry-pots, which, covered with the parchment-like poke or stomach skin of\nthe black fish, gave forth a loud roar to every stroke of the clenched\nhands of the crew. On the quarter-deck, the mates and harpooneers were\ndancing with the olive-hued girls who had eloped with them from the\nPolynesian Isles; while suspended in an ornamented boat, firmly secured\naloft between the foremast and mainmast, three Long Island negroes, with\nglittering fiddle-bows of whale ivory, were presiding over the hilarious\njig. Meanwhile, others of the ship\u2019s company were tumultuously busy at\nthe masonry of the try-works, from which the huge pots had been\nremoved. You would have almost thought they were pulling down the cursed\nBastille, such wild cries they raised, as the now useless brick and\nmortar were being hurled into the sea.\n\nLord and master over all this scene, the captain stood erect on the\nship\u2019s elevated quarter-deck, so that the whole rejoicing drama was\nfull before him, and seemed merely contrived for his own individual\ndiversion.\n\nAnd Ahab, he too was standing on his quarter-deck, shaggy and black,\nwith a stubborn gloom; and as the two ships crossed each other\u2019s\nwakes\u2014one all jubilations for things passed, the other all forebodings\nas to things to come\u2014their two captains in themselves impersonated the\nwhole striking contrast of the scene.\n\n\u201cCome aboard, come aboard!\u201d cried the gay Bachelor\u2019s commander,\nlifting a glass and a bottle in the air.\n\n\u201cHast seen the White Whale?\u201d gritted Ahab in reply.\n\n\u201cNo; only heard of him; but don\u2019t believe in him at all,\u201d said the\nother good-humoredly. \u201cCome aboard!\u201d\n\n\u201cThou art too damned jolly. Sail on. Hast lost any men?\u201d\n\n\u201cNot enough to speak of\u2014two islanders, that\u2019s all;\u2014but come\naboard, old hearty, come along. I\u2019ll soon take that black from\nyour brow. Come along, will ye (merry\u2019s the play); a full ship and\nhomeward-bound.\u201d\n\n\u201cHow wondrous familiar is a fool!\u201d muttered Ahab; then aloud,\n\u201cThou art a full ship and homeward bound, thou sayst; well, then, call\nme an empty ship, and outward-bound. So go thy ways, and I will mine.\nForward there! Set all sail, and keep her to the wind!\u201d\n\nAnd thus, while the one ship went cheerily before the breeze, the other\nstubbornly fought against it; and so the two vessels parted; the crew\nof the Pequod looking with grave, lingering glances towards the receding\nBachelor; but the Bachelor\u2019s men never heeding their gaze for the\nlively revelry they were in. And as Ahab, leaning over the taffrail,\neyed the homewardbound craft, he took from his pocket a small vial\nof sand, and then looking from the ship to the vial, seemed thereby\nbringing two remote associations together, for that vial was filled with\nNantucket soundings.\n\n\n\n\n\nCHAPTER 116. The Dying Whale.\n\nNot seldom in this life, when, on the right side, fortune\u2019s favourites\nsail close by us, we, though all adroop before, catch somewhat of the\nrushing breeze, and joyfully feel our bagging sails fill out. So seemed\nit with the Pequod. For next day after encountering the gay Bachelor,\nwhales were seen and four were slain; and one of them by Ahab.\n\nIt was far down the afternoon; and when all the spearings of the crimson\nfight were done: and floating in the lovely sunset sea and sky, sun\nand whale both stilly died together; then, such a sweetness and such\nplaintiveness, such inwreathing orisons curled up in that rosy air, that\nit almost seemed as if far over from the deep green convent valleys of\nthe Manilla isles, the Spanish land-breeze, wantonly turned sailor, had\ngone to sea, freighted with these vesper hymns.\n\nSoothed again, but only soothed to deeper gloom, Ahab, who had sterned\noff from the whale, sat intently watching his final wanings from the now\ntranquil boat. For that strange spectacle observable in all sperm whales\ndying\u2014the turning sunwards of the head, and so expiring\u2014that strange\nspectacle, beheld of such a placid evening, somehow to Ahab conveyed a\nwondrousness unknown before.\n\n\u201cHe turns and turns him to it,\u2014how slowly, but how steadfastly, his\nhomage-rendering and invoking brow, with his last dying motions. He too\nworships fire; most faithful, broad, baronial vassal of the sun!\u2014Oh\nthat these too-favouring eyes should see these too-favouring sights.\nLook! here, far water-locked; beyond all hum of human weal or woe;\nin these most candid and impartial seas; where to traditions no rocks\nfurnish tablets; where for long Chinese ages, the billows have still\nrolled on speechless and unspoken to, as stars that shine upon the\nNiger\u2019s unknown source; here, too, life dies sunwards full of faith;\nbut see! no sooner dead, than death whirls round the corpse, and it\nheads some other way.\n\n\u201cOh, thou dark Hindoo half of nature, who of drowned bones hast\nbuilded thy separate throne somewhere in the heart of these unverdured\nseas; thou art an infidel, thou queen, and too truly speakest to me in\nthe wide-slaughtering Typhoon, and the hushed burial of its after calm.\nNor has this thy whale sunwards turned his dying head, and then gone\nround again, without a lesson to me.\n\n\u201cOh, trebly hooped and welded hip of power! Oh, high aspiring,\nrainbowed jet!\u2014that one strivest, this one jettest all in vain! In\nvain, oh whale, dost thou seek intercedings with yon all-quickening\nsun, that only calls forth life, but gives it not again. Yet dost\nthou, darker half, rock me with a prouder, if a darker faith. All thy\nunnamable imminglings float beneath me here; I am buoyed by breaths of\nonce living things, exhaled as air, but water now.\n\n\u201cThen hail, for ever hail, O sea, in whose eternal tossings the wild\nfowl finds his only rest. Born of earth, yet suckled by the sea; though\nhill and valley mothered me, ye billows are my foster-brothers!\u201d\n\n\n\n\n\nCHAPTER 117. The Whale Watch.\n\nThe four whales slain that evening had died wide apart; one, far to\nwindward; one, less distant, to leeward; one ahead; one astern. These\nlast three were brought alongside ere nightfall; but the windward one\ncould not be reached till morning; and the boat that had killed it lay\nby its side all night; and that boat was Ahab\u2019s.\n\nThe waif-pole was thrust upright into the dead whale\u2019s spout-hole; and\nthe lantern hanging from its top, cast a troubled flickering glare\nupon the black, glossy back, and far out upon the midnight waves, which\ngently chafed the whale\u2019s broad flank, like soft surf upon a beach.\n\nAhab and all his boat\u2019s crew seemed asleep but the Parsee; who\ncrouching in the bow, sat watching the sharks, that spectrally played\nround the whale, and tapped the light cedar planks with their tails.\nA sound like the moaning in squadrons over Asphaltites of unforgiven\nghosts of Gomorrah, ran shuddering through the air.\n\nStarted from his slumbers, Ahab, face to face, saw the Parsee; and\nhooped round by the gloom of the night they seemed the last men in a\nflooded world. \u201cI have dreamed it again,\u201d said he.\n\n\u201cOf the hearses? Have I not said, old man, that neither hearse nor\ncoffin can be thine?\u201d\n\n\u201cAnd who are hearsed that die on the sea?\u201d\n\n\u201cBut I said, old man, that ere thou couldst die on this voyage, two\nhearses must verily be seen by thee on the sea; the first not made by\nmortal hands; and the visible wood of the last one must be grown in\nAmerica.\u201d\n\n\u201cAye, aye! a strange sight that, Parsee:\u2014a hearse and its plumes\nfloating over the ocean with the waves for the pall-bearers. Ha! Such a\nsight we shall not soon see.\u201d\n\n\u201cBelieve it or not, thou canst not die till it be seen, old man.\u201d\n\n\u201cAnd what was that saying about thyself?\u201d\n\n\u201cThough it come to the last, I shall still go before thee thy\npilot.\u201d\n\n\u201cAnd when thou art so gone before\u2014if that ever befall\u2014then ere I\ncan follow, thou must still appear to me, to pilot me still?\u2014Was it\nnot so? Well, then, did I believe all ye say, oh my pilot! I have here\ntwo pledges that I shall yet slay Moby Dick and survive it.\u201d\n\n\u201cTake another pledge, old man,\u201d said the Parsee, as his eyes lighted\nup like fire-flies in the gloom\u2014\u201cHemp only can kill thee.\u201d\n\n\u201cThe gallows, ye mean.\u2014I am immortal then, on land and on sea,\u201d\ncried Ahab, with a laugh of derision;\u2014\u201cImmortal on land and on\nsea!\u201d\n\nBoth were silent again, as one man. The grey dawn came on, and the\nslumbering crew arose from the boat\u2019s bottom, and ere noon the dead\nwhale was brought to the ship.\n\n\n\n\n\nCHAPTER 118. The Quadrant.\n\nThe season for the Line at length drew near; and every day when Ahab,\ncoming from his cabin, cast his eyes aloft, the vigilant helmsman would\nostentatiously handle his spokes, and the eager mariners quickly run to\nthe braces, and would stand there with all their eyes centrally fixed on\nthe nailed doubloon; impatient for the order to point the ship\u2019s prow\nfor the equator. In good time the order came. It was hard upon high\nnoon; and Ahab, seated in the bows of his high-hoisted boat, was\nabout taking his wonted daily observation of the sun to determine his\nlatitude.\n\nNow, in that Japanese sea, the days in summer are as freshets of\neffulgences. That unblinkingly vivid Japanese sun seems the blazing\nfocus of the glassy ocean\u2019s immeasurable burning-glass. The sky looks\nlacquered; clouds there are none; the horizon floats; and this nakedness\nof unrelieved radiance is as the insufferable splendors of God\u2019s\nthrone. Well that Ahab\u2019s quadrant was furnished with coloured glasses,\nthrough which to take sight of that solar fire. So, swinging his\nseated form to the roll of the ship, and with his astrological-looking\ninstrument placed to his eye, he remained in that posture for some\nmoments to catch the precise instant when the sun should gain its\nprecise meridian. Meantime while his whole attention was absorbed, the\nParsee was kneeling beneath him on the ship\u2019s deck, and with face\nthrown up like Ahab\u2019s, was eyeing the same sun with him; only the lids\nof his eyes half hooded their orbs, and his wild face was subdued to an\nearthly passionlessness. At length the desired observation was taken;\nand with his pencil upon his ivory leg, Ahab soon calculated what his\nlatitude must be at that precise instant. Then falling into a moment\u2019s\nrevery, he again looked up towards the sun and murmured to himself:\n\u201cThou sea-mark! thou high and mighty Pilot! thou tellest me truly\nwhere I am\u2014but canst thou cast the least hint where I shall be? Or\ncanst thou tell where some other thing besides me is this moment living?\nWhere is Moby Dick? This instant thou must be eyeing him. These eyes\nof mine look into the very eye that is even now beholding him; aye,\nand into the eye that is even now equally beholding the objects on the\nunknown, thither side of thee, thou sun!\u201d\n\nThen gazing at his quadrant, and handling, one after the other, its\nnumerous cabalistical contrivances, he pondered again, and muttered:\n\u201cFoolish toy! babies\u2019 plaything of haughty Admirals, and Commodores,\nand Captains; the world brags of thee, of thy cunning and might; but\nwhat after all canst thou do, but tell the poor, pitiful point, where\nthou thyself happenest to be on this wide planet, and the hand that\nholds thee: no! not one jot more! Thou canst not tell where one drop\nof water or one grain of sand will be to-morrow noon; and yet with thy\nimpotence thou insultest the sun! Science! Curse thee, thou vain toy;\nand cursed be all the things that cast man\u2019s eyes aloft to that\nheaven, whose live vividness but scorches him, as these old eyes\nare even now scorched with thy light, O sun! Level by nature to this\nearth\u2019s horizon are the glances of man\u2019s eyes; not shot from the\ncrown of his head, as if God had meant him to gaze on his firmament.\nCurse thee, thou quadrant!\u201d dashing it to the deck, \u201cno longer will\nI guide my earthly way by thee; the level ship\u2019s compass, and the\nlevel deadreckoning, by log and by line; these shall conduct me, and\nshow me my place on the sea. Aye,\u201d lighting from the boat to the deck,\n\u201cthus I trample on thee, thou paltry thing that feebly pointest on\nhigh; thus I split and destroy thee!\u201d\n\nAs the frantic old man thus spoke and thus trampled with his live\nand dead feet, a sneering triumph that seemed meant for Ahab, and a\nfatalistic despair that seemed meant for himself\u2014these passed over the\nmute, motionless Parsee\u2019s face. Unobserved he rose and glided away;\nwhile, awestruck by the aspect of their commander, the seamen clustered\ntogether on the forecastle, till Ahab, troubledly pacing the deck,\nshouted out\u2014\u201cTo the braces! Up helm!\u2014square in!\u201d\n\nIn an instant the yards swung round; and as the ship half-wheeled upon\nher heel, her three firm-seated graceful masts erectly poised upon\nher long, ribbed hull, seemed as the three Horatii pirouetting on one\nsufficient steed.\n\nStanding between the knight-heads, Starbuck watched the Pequod\u2019s\ntumultuous way, and Ahab\u2019s also, as he went lurching along the deck.\n\n\u201cI have sat before the dense coal fire and watched it all aglow, full\nof its tormented flaming life; and I have seen it wane at last, down,\ndown, to dumbest dust. Old man of oceans! of all this fiery life of\nthine, what will at length remain but one little heap of ashes!\u201d\n\n\u201cAye,\u201d cried Stubb, \u201cbut sea-coal ashes\u2014mind ye that, Mr.\nStarbuck\u2014sea-coal, not your common charcoal. Well, well; I heard Ahab\nmutter, \u2018Here some one thrusts these cards into these old hands of\nmine; swears that I must play them, and no others.\u2019 And damn me, Ahab,\nbut thou actest right; live in the game, and die in it!\u201d\n\n\n\n\n\nCHAPTER 119. The Candles.\n\nWarmest climes but nurse the cruellest fangs: the tiger of Bengal\ncrouches in spiced groves of ceaseless verdure. Skies the most effulgent\nbut basket the deadliest thunders: gorgeous Cuba knows tornadoes\nthat never swept tame northern lands. So, too, it is, that in these\nresplendent Japanese seas the mariner encounters the direst of all\nstorms, the Typhoon. It will sometimes burst from out that cloudless\nsky, like an exploding bomb upon a dazed and sleepy town.\n\nTowards evening of that day, the Pequod was torn of her canvas, and\nbare-poled was left to fight a Typhoon which had struck her directly\nahead. When darkness came on, sky and sea roared and split with the\nthunder, and blazed with the lightning, that showed the disabled masts\nfluttering here and there with the rags which the first fury of the\ntempest had left for its after sport.\n\nHolding by a shroud, Starbuck was standing on the quarter-deck; at every\nflash of the lightning glancing aloft, to see what additional disaster\nmight have befallen the intricate hamper there; while Stubb and Flask\nwere directing the men in the higher hoisting and firmer lashing of the\nboats. But all their pains seemed naught. Though lifted to the very top\nof the cranes, the windward quarter boat (Ahab\u2019s) did not escape. A\ngreat rolling sea, dashing high up against the reeling ship\u2019s high\nteetering side, stove in the boat\u2019s bottom at the stern, and left it\nagain, all dripping through like a sieve.\n\n\u201cBad work, bad work! Mr. Starbuck,\u201d said Stubb, regarding the wreck,\n\u201cbut the sea will have its way. Stubb, for one, can\u2019t fight it. You\nsee, Mr. Starbuck, a wave has such a great long start before it leaps,\nall round the world it runs, and then comes the spring! But as for me,\nall the start I have to meet it, is just across the deck here. But never\nmind; it\u2019s all in fun: so the old song says;\u201d\u2014(sings.)\n\n  Oh! jolly is the gale,\n  And a joker is the whale,\n  A\u2019 flourishin\u2019 his tail,\u2014\n  Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh!\n\n  The scud all a flyin\u2019,\n  That\u2019s his flip only foamin\u2019;\n  When he stirs in the spicin\u2019,\u2014\n  Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh!\n\n  Thunder splits the ships,\n  But he only smacks his lips,\n  A tastin\u2019 of this flip,\u2014\n  Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh!\n\n\u201cAvast Stubb,\u201d cried Starbuck, \u201clet the Typhoon sing, and strike\nhis harp here in our rigging; but if thou art a brave man thou wilt hold\nthy peace.\u201d\n\n\u201cBut I am not a brave man; never said I was a brave man; I am a\ncoward; and I sing to keep up my spirits. And I tell you what it is, Mr.\nStarbuck, there\u2019s no way to stop my singing in this world but to cut\nmy throat. And when that\u2019s done, ten to one I sing ye the doxology for\na wind-up.\u201d\n\n\u201cMadman! look through my eyes if thou hast none of thine own.\u201d\n\n\u201cWhat! how can you see better of a dark night than anybody else, never\nmind how foolish?\u201d\n\n\u201cHere!\u201d cried Starbuck, seizing Stubb by the shoulder, and pointing\nhis hand towards the weather bow, \u201cmarkest thou not that the gale\ncomes from the eastward, the very course Ahab is to run for Moby Dick?\nthe very course he swung to this day noon? now mark his boat there;\nwhere is that stove? In the stern-sheets, man; where he is wont to\nstand\u2014his stand-point is stove, man! Now jump overboard, and sing\naway, if thou must!\n\n\u201cI don\u2019t half understand ye: what\u2019s in the wind?\u201d\n\n\u201cYes, yes, round the Cape of Good Hope is the shortest way to\nNantucket,\u201d soliloquized Starbuck suddenly, heedless of Stubb\u2019s\nquestion. \u201cThe gale that now hammers at us to stave us, we can turn it\ninto a fair wind that will drive us towards home. Yonder, to windward,\nall is blackness of doom; but to leeward, homeward\u2014I see it lightens\nup there; but not with the lightning.\u201d\n\nAt that moment in one of the intervals of profound darkness, following\nthe flashes, a voice was heard at his side; and almost at the same\ninstant a volley of thunder peals rolled overhead.\n\n\u201cWho\u2019s there?\u201d\n\n\u201cOld Thunder!\u201d said Ahab, groping his way along the bulwarks to his\npivot-hole; but suddenly finding his path made plain to him by elbowed\nlances of fire.\n\nNow, as the lightning rod to a spire on shore is intended to carry off\nthe perilous fluid into the soil; so the kindred rod which at sea some\nships carry to each mast, is intended to conduct it into the water. But\nas this conductor must descend to considerable depth, that its end may\navoid all contact with the hull; and as moreover, if kept constantly\ntowing there, it would be liable to many mishaps, besides interfering\nnot a little with some of the rigging, and more or less impeding the\nvessel\u2019s way in the water; because of all this, the lower parts of a\nship\u2019s lightning-rods are not always overboard; but are generally made\nin long slender links, so as to be the more readily hauled up into the\nchains outside, or thrown down into the sea, as occasion may require.\n\n\u201cThe rods! the rods!\u201d cried Starbuck to the crew, suddenly\nadmonished to vigilance by the vivid lightning that had just been\ndarting flambeaux, to light Ahab to his post. \u201cAre they overboard?\ndrop them over, fore and aft. Quick!\u201d\n\n\u201cAvast!\u201d cried Ahab; \u201clet\u2019s have fair play here, though we be\nthe weaker side. Yet I\u2019ll contribute to raise rods on the Himmalehs\nand Andes, that all the world may be secured; but out on privileges! Let\nthem be, sir.\u201d\n\n\u201cLook aloft!\u201d cried Starbuck. \u201cThe corpusants! the corpusants!\u201d\n\nAll the yard-arms were tipped with a pallid fire; and touched at each\ntri-pointed lightning-rod-end with three tapering white flames, each of\nthe three tall masts was silently burning in that sulphurous air, like\nthree gigantic wax tapers before an altar.\n\n\u201cBlast the boat! let it go!\u201d cried Stubb at this instant, as a\nswashing sea heaved up under his own little craft, so that its gunwale\nviolently jammed his hand, as he was passing a lashing. \u201cBlast\nit!\u201d\u2014but slipping backward on the deck, his uplifted eyes caught the\nflames; and immediately shifting his tone he cried\u2014\u201cThe corpusants\nhave mercy on us all!\u201d\n\nTo sailors, oaths are household words; they will swear in the trance of\nthe calm, and in the teeth of the tempest; they will imprecate curses\nfrom the topsail-yard-arms, when most they teeter over to a seething\nsea; but in all my voyagings, seldom have I heard a common oath when\nGod\u2019s burning finger has been laid on the ship; when His \u201cMene,\nMene, Tekel Upharsin\u201d has been woven into the shrouds and the cordage.\n\nWhile this pallidness was burning aloft, few words were heard from the\nenchanted crew; who in one thick cluster stood on the forecastle,\nall their eyes gleaming in that pale phosphorescence, like a far away\nconstellation of stars. Relieved against the ghostly light, the gigantic\njet negro, Daggoo, loomed up to thrice his real stature, and seemed\nthe black cloud from which the thunder had come. The parted mouth of\nTashtego revealed his shark-white teeth, which strangely gleamed as\nif they too had been tipped by corpusants; while lit up by the\npreternatural light, Queequeg\u2019s tattooing burned like Satanic blue\nflames on his body.\n\nThe tableau all waned at last with the pallidness aloft; and once more\nthe Pequod and every soul on her decks were wrapped in a pall. A moment\nor two passed, when Starbuck, going forward, pushed against some one. It\nwas Stubb. \u201cWhat thinkest thou now, man; I heard thy cry; it was not\nthe same in the song.\u201d\n\n\u201cNo, no, it wasn\u2019t; I said the corpusants have mercy on us all;\nand I hope they will, still. But do they only have mercy on\nlong faces?\u2014have they no bowels for a laugh? And look ye, Mr.\nStarbuck\u2014but it\u2019s too dark to look. Hear me, then: I take that\nmast-head flame we saw for a sign of good luck; for those masts are\nrooted in a hold that is going to be chock a\u2019 block with sperm-oil,\nd\u2019ye see; and so, all that sperm will work up into the masts, like\nsap in a tree. Yes, our three masts will yet be as three spermaceti\ncandles\u2014that\u2019s the good promise we saw.\u201d\n\nAt that moment Starbuck caught sight of Stubb\u2019s face slowly beginning\nto glimmer into sight. Glancing upwards, he cried: \u201cSee! see!\u201d\nand once more the high tapering flames were beheld with what seemed\nredoubled supernaturalness in their pallor.\n\n\u201cThe corpusants have mercy on us all,\u201d cried Stubb, again.\n\nAt the base of the mainmast, full beneath the doubloon and the flame,\nthe Parsee was kneeling in Ahab\u2019s front, but with his head bowed away\nfrom him; while near by, from the arched and overhanging rigging, where\nthey had just been engaged securing a spar, a number of the seamen,\narrested by the glare, now cohered together, and hung pendulous, like a\nknot of numbed wasps from a drooping, orchard twig. In various enchanted\nattitudes, like the standing, or stepping, or running skeletons in\nHerculaneum, others remained rooted to the deck; but all their eyes\nupcast.\n\n\u201cAye, aye, men!\u201d cried Ahab. \u201cLook up at it; mark it well;\nthe white flame but lights the way to the White Whale! Hand me those\nmainmast links there; I would fain feel this pulse, and let mine beat\nagainst it; blood against fire! So.\u201d\n\nThen turning\u2014the last link held fast in his left hand, he put his foot\nupon the Parsee; and with fixed upward eye, and high-flung right arm, he\nstood erect before the lofty tri-pointed trinity of flames.\n\n\u201cOh! thou clear spirit of clear fire, whom on these seas I as Persian\nonce did worship, till in the sacramental act so burned by thee, that to\nthis hour I bear the scar; I now know thee, thou clear spirit, and I now\nknow that thy right worship is defiance. To neither love nor reverence\nwilt thou be kind; and e\u2019en for hate thou canst but kill; and all\nare killed. No fearless fool now fronts thee. I own thy speechless,\nplaceless power; but to the last gasp of my earthquake life will\ndispute its unconditional, unintegral mastery in me. In the midst of the\npersonified impersonal, a personality stands here. Though but a point\nat best; whencesoe\u2019er I came; wheresoe\u2019er I go; yet while I earthly\nlive, the queenly personality lives in me, and feels her royal rights.\nBut war is pain, and hate is woe. Come in thy lowest form of love, and\nI will kneel and kiss thee; but at thy highest, come as mere supernal\npower; and though thou launchest navies of full-freighted worlds,\nthere\u2019s that in here that still remains indifferent. Oh, thou clear\nspirit, of thy fire thou madest me, and like a true child of fire, I\nbreathe it back to thee.\u201d\n\n[Sudden, repeated flashes of lightning; the nine flames leap lengthwise\nto thrice their previous height; Ahab, with the rest, closes his eyes,\nhis right hand pressed hard upon them.]\n\n\u201cI own thy speechless, placeless power; said I not so? Nor was it\nwrung from me; nor do I now drop these links. Thou canst blind; but I\ncan then grope. Thou canst consume; but I can then be ashes. Take the\nhomage of these poor eyes, and shutter-hands. I would not take it. The\nlightning flashes through my skull; mine eye-balls ache and ache; my\nwhole beaten brain seems as beheaded, and rolling on some stunning\nground. Oh, oh! Yet blindfold, yet will I talk to thee. Light though\nthou be, thou leapest out of darkness; but I am darkness leaping out of\nlight, leaping out of thee! The javelins cease; open eyes; see, or\nnot? There burn the flames! Oh, thou magnanimous! now I do glory in my\ngenealogy. But thou art but my fiery father; my sweet mother, I know\nnot. Oh, cruel! what hast thou done with her? There lies my puzzle; but\nthine is greater. Thou knowest not how came ye, hence callest thyself\nunbegotten; certainly knowest not thy beginning, hence callest thyself\nunbegun. I know that of me, which thou knowest not of thyself, oh, thou\nomnipotent. There is some unsuffusing thing beyond thee, thou clear\nspirit, to whom all thy eternity is but time, all thy creativeness\nmechanical. Through thee, thy flaming self, my scorched eyes do dimly\nsee it. Oh, thou foundling fire, thou hermit immemorial, thou too hast\nthy incommunicable riddle, thy unparticipated grief. Here again with\nhaughty agony, I read my sire. Leap! leap up, and lick the sky! I leap\nwith thee; I burn with thee; would fain be welded with thee; defyingly I\nworship thee!\u201d\n\n\u201cThe boat! the boat!\u201d cried Starbuck, \u201clook at thy boat, old\nman!\u201d\n\nAhab\u2019s harpoon, the one forged at Perth\u2019s fire, remained firmly\nlashed in its conspicuous crotch, so that it projected beyond his\nwhale-boat\u2019s bow; but the sea that had stove its bottom had caused the\nloose leather sheath to drop off; and from the keen steel barb there now\ncame a levelled flame of pale, forked fire. As the silent harpoon\nburned there like a serpent\u2019s tongue, Starbuck grasped Ahab by the\narm\u2014\u201cGod, God is against thee, old man; forbear! \u2018tis an ill\nvoyage! ill begun, ill continued; let me square the yards, while we may,\nold man, and make a fair wind of it homewards, to go on a better voyage\nthan this.\u201d\n\nOverhearing Starbuck, the panic-stricken crew instantly ran to the\nbraces\u2014though not a sail was left aloft. For the moment all the aghast\nmate\u2019s thoughts seemed theirs; they raised a half mutinous cry. But\ndashing the rattling lightning links to the deck, and snatching the\nburning harpoon, Ahab waved it like a torch among them; swearing to\ntransfix with it the first sailor that but cast loose a rope\u2019s end.\nPetrified by his aspect, and still more shrinking from the fiery dart\nthat he held, the men fell back in dismay, and Ahab again spoke:\u2014\n\n\u201cAll your oaths to hunt the White Whale are as binding as mine; and\nheart, soul, and body, lungs and life, old Ahab is bound. And that ye\nmay know to what tune this heart beats; look ye here; thus I blow out\nthe last fear!\u201d And with one blast of his breath he extinguished the\nflame.\n\nAs in the hurricane that sweeps the plain, men fly the neighborhood of\nsome lone, gigantic elm, whose very height and strength but render it so\nmuch the more unsafe, because so much the more a mark for thunderbolts;\nso at those last words of Ahab\u2019s many of the mariners did run from him\nin a terror of dismay.\n\n\n\n\n\nCHAPTER 120. The Deck Towards the End of the First Night Watch. Ahab\nstanding by the helm. Starbuck approaching him.\n\n\u201cWe must send down the main-top-sail yard, sir. The band is working\nloose and the lee lift is half-stranded. Shall I strike it, sir?\u201d\n\n\u201cStrike nothing; lash it. If I had sky-sail poles, I\u2019d sway them up\nnow.\u201d\n\n\u201cSir!\u2014in God\u2019s name!\u2014sir?\u201d\n\n\u201cWell.\u201d\n\n\u201cThe anchors are working, sir. Shall I get them inboard?\u201d\n\n\u201cStrike nothing, and stir nothing, but lash everything. The wind\nrises, but it has not got up to my table-lands yet. Quick, and see to\nit.\u2014By masts and keels! he takes me for the hunch-backed skipper of\nsome coasting smack. Send down my main-top-sail yard! Ho, gluepots!\nLoftiest trucks were made for wildest winds, and this brain-truck of\nmine now sails amid the cloud-scud. Shall I strike that? Oh, none but\ncowards send down their brain-trucks in tempest time. What a hooroosh\naloft there! I would e\u2019en take it for sublime, did I not know that the\ncolic is a noisy malady. Oh, take medicine, take medicine!\u201d\n\n\n\n\n\nCHAPTER 121. Midnight.\u2014The Forecastle Bulwarks.\n\nStubb and Flask mounted on them, and passing additional lashings over\nthe anchors there hanging.\n\n\u201cNo, Stubb; you may pound that knot there as much as you please, but\nyou will never pound into me what you were just now saying. And how long\nago is it since you said the very contrary? Didn\u2019t you once say that\nwhatever ship Ahab sails in, that ship should pay something extra on its\ninsurance policy, just as though it were loaded with powder barrels aft\nand boxes of lucifers forward? Stop, now; didn\u2019t you say so?\u201d\n\n\u201cWell, suppose I did? What then? I\u2019ve part changed my flesh since\nthat time, why not my mind? Besides, supposing we are loaded with powder\nbarrels aft and lucifers forward; how the devil could the lucifers get\nafire in this drenching spray here? Why, my little man, you have pretty\nred hair, but you couldn\u2019t get afire now. Shake yourself; you\u2019re\nAquarius, or the water-bearer, Flask; might fill pitchers at your coat\ncollar. Don\u2019t you see, then, that for these extra risks the Marine\nInsurance companies have extra guarantees? Here are hydrants, Flask. But\nhark, again, and I\u2019ll answer ye the other thing. First take your leg\noff from the crown of the anchor here, though, so I can pass the rope;\nnow listen. What\u2019s the mighty difference between holding a mast\u2019s\nlightning-rod in the storm, and standing close by a mast that\nhasn\u2019t got any lightning-rod at all in a storm? Don\u2019t you see, you\ntimber-head, that no harm can come to the holder of the rod, unless the\nmast is first struck? What are you talking about, then? Not one ship in\na hundred carries rods, and Ahab,\u2014aye, man, and all of us,\u2014were\nin no more danger then, in my poor opinion, than all the crews in ten\nthousand ships now sailing the seas. Why, you King-Post, you, I\nsuppose you would have every man in the world go about with a small\nlightning-rod running up the corner of his hat, like a militia\nofficer\u2019s skewered feather, and trailing behind like his sash. Why\ndon\u2019t ye be sensible, Flask? it\u2019s easy to be sensible; why don\u2019t\nye, then? any man with half an eye can be sensible.\u201d\n\n\u201cI don\u2019t know that, Stubb. You sometimes find it rather hard.\u201d\n\n\u201cYes, when a fellow\u2019s soaked through, it\u2019s hard to be sensible,\nthat\u2019s a fact. And I am about drenched with this spray. Never mind;\ncatch the turn there, and pass it. Seems to me we are lashing down these\nanchors now as if they were never going to be used again. Tying these\ntwo anchors here, Flask, seems like tying a man\u2019s hands behind him.\nAnd what big generous hands they are, to be sure. These are your iron\nfists, hey? What a hold they have, too! I wonder, Flask, whether the\nworld is anchored anywhere; if she is, she swings with an uncommon long\ncable, though. There, hammer that knot down, and we\u2019ve done. So; next\nto touching land, lighting on deck is the most satisfactory. I say, just\nwring out my jacket skirts, will ye? Thank ye. They laugh at long-togs\nso, Flask; but seems to me, a Long tailed coat ought always to be worn\nin all storms afloat. The tails tapering down that way, serve to\ncarry off the water, d\u2019ye see. Same with cocked hats; the cocks form\ngable-end eave-troughs, Flask. No more monkey-jackets and tarpaulins for\nme; I must mount a swallow-tail, and drive down a beaver; so. Halloa!\nwhew! there goes my tarpaulin overboard; Lord, Lord, that the winds that\ncome from heaven should be so unmannerly! This is a nasty night, lad.\u201d\n\n\n\n\n\nCHAPTER 122. Midnight Aloft.\u2014Thunder and Lightning.\n\nThe main-top-sail yard.\u2014Tashtego passing new lashings around it.\n\n\u201cUm, um, um. Stop that thunder! Plenty too much thunder up here.\nWhat\u2019s the use of thunder? Um, um, um. We don\u2019t want thunder; we\nwant rum; give us a glass of rum. Um, um, um!\u201d\n\n\n\n\n\nCHAPTER 123. The Musket.\n\nDuring the most violent shocks of the Typhoon, the man at the Pequod\u2019s\njaw-bone tiller had several times been reelingly hurled to the deck by\nits spasmodic motions, even though preventer tackles had been attached\nto it\u2014for they were slack\u2014because some play to the tiller was\nindispensable.\n\nIn a severe gale like this, while the ship is but a tossed shuttlecock\nto the blast, it is by no means uncommon to see the needles in the\ncompasses, at intervals, go round and round. It was thus with the\nPequod\u2019s; at almost every shock the helmsman had not failed to notice\nthe whirling velocity with which they revolved upon the cards; it is\na sight that hardly anyone can behold without some sort of unwonted\nemotion.\n\nSome hours after midnight, the Typhoon abated so much, that through the\nstrenuous exertions of Starbuck and Stubb\u2014one engaged forward and the\nother aft\u2014the shivered remnants of the jib and fore and main-top-sails\nwere cut adrift from the spars, and went eddying away to leeward, like\nthe feathers of an albatross, which sometimes are cast to the winds when\nthat storm-tossed bird is on the wing.\n\nThe three corresponding new sails were now bent and reefed, and a\nstorm-trysail was set further aft; so that the ship soon went through\nthe water with some precision again; and the course\u2014for the present,\nEast-south-east\u2014which he was to steer, if practicable, was once more\ngiven to the helmsman. For during the violence of the gale, he had only\nsteered according to its vicissitudes. But as he was now bringing the\nship as near her course as possible, watching the compass meanwhile, lo!\na good sign! the wind seemed coming round astern; aye, the foul breeze\nbecame fair!\n\nInstantly the yards were squared, to the lively song of \u201cHo! the\nfair wind! oh-ye-ho, cheerly men!\u201d the crew singing for joy, that\nso promising an event should so soon have falsified the evil portents\npreceding it.\n\nIn compliance with the standing order of his commander\u2014to report\nimmediately, and at any one of the twenty-four hours, any decided change\nin the affairs of the deck,\u2014Starbuck had no sooner trimmed the yards\nto the breeze\u2014however reluctantly and gloomily,\u2014than he mechanically\nwent below to apprise Captain Ahab of the circumstance.\n\nEre knocking at his state-room, he involuntarily paused before it a\nmoment. The cabin lamp\u2014taking long swings this way and that\u2014was\nburning fitfully, and casting fitful shadows upon the old man\u2019s\nbolted door,\u2014a thin one, with fixed blinds inserted, in place of\nupper panels. The isolated subterraneousness of the cabin made a certain\nhumming silence to reign there, though it was hooped round by all the\nroar of the elements. The loaded muskets in the rack were shiningly\nrevealed, as they stood upright against the forward bulkhead. Starbuck\nwas an honest, upright man; but out of Starbuck\u2019s heart, at that\ninstant when he saw the muskets, there strangely evolved an evil\nthought; but so blent with its neutral or good accompaniments that for\nthe instant he hardly knew it for itself.\n\n\u201cHe would have shot me once,\u201d he murmured, \u201cyes, there\u2019s the\nvery musket that he pointed at me;\u2014that one with the studded stock;\nlet me touch it\u2014lift it. Strange, that I, who have handled so many\ndeadly lances, strange, that I should shake so now. Loaded? I must\nsee. Aye, aye; and powder in the pan;\u2014that\u2019s not good. Best spill\nit?\u2014wait. I\u2019ll cure myself of this. I\u2019ll hold the musket boldly\nwhile I think.\u2014I come to report a fair wind to him. But how fair? Fair\nfor death and doom,\u2014that\u2019s fair for Moby Dick. It\u2019s a fair wind\nthat\u2019s only fair for that accursed fish.\u2014The very tube he pointed at\nme!\u2014the very one; this one\u2014I hold it here; he would have killed me\nwith the very thing I handle now.\u2014Aye and he would fain kill all his\ncrew. Does he not say he will not strike his spars to any gale? Has\nhe not dashed his heavenly quadrant? and in these same perilous seas,\ngropes he not his way by mere dead reckoning of the error-abounding\nlog? and in this very Typhoon, did he not swear that he would have no\nlightning-rods? But shall this crazed old man be tamely suffered to drag\na whole ship\u2019s company down to doom with him?\u2014Yes, it would make\nhim the wilful murderer of thirty men and more, if this ship come to any\ndeadly harm; and come to deadly harm, my soul swears this ship will,\nif Ahab have his way. If, then, he were this instant\u2014put aside, that\ncrime would not be his. Ha! is he muttering in his sleep? Yes, just\nthere,\u2014in there, he\u2019s sleeping. Sleeping? aye, but still alive,\nand soon awake again. I can\u2019t withstand thee, then, old man. Not\nreasoning; not remonstrance; not entreaty wilt thou hearken to; all this\nthou scornest. Flat obedience to thy own flat commands, this is all thou\nbreathest. Aye, and say\u2019st the men have vow\u2019d thy vow; say\u2019st\nall of us are Ahabs. Great God forbid!\u2014But is there no other way? no\nlawful way?\u2014Make him a prisoner to be taken home? What! hope to wrest\nthis old man\u2019s living power from his own living hands? Only a fool\nwould try it. Say he were pinioned even; knotted all over with ropes\nand hawsers; chained down to ring-bolts on this cabin floor; he would\nbe more hideous than a caged tiger, then. I could not endure the\nsight; could not possibly fly his howlings; all comfort, sleep itself,\ninestimable reason would leave me on the long intolerable voyage. What,\nthen, remains? The land is hundreds of leagues away, and locked Japan\nthe nearest. I stand alone here upon an open sea, with two oceans and a\nwhole continent between me and law.\u2014Aye, aye, \u2018tis so.\u2014Is heaven\na murderer when its lightning strikes a would-be murderer in his bed,\ntindering sheets and skin together?\u2014And would I be a murderer, then,\nif\u201d\u2014and slowly, stealthily, and half sideways looking, he placed the\nloaded musket\u2019s end against the door.\n\n\u201cOn this level, Ahab\u2019s hammock swings within; his head this way. A\ntouch, and Starbuck may survive to hug his wife and child again.\u2014Oh\nMary! Mary!\u2014boy! boy! boy!\u2014But if I wake thee not to death, old man,\nwho can tell to what unsounded deeps Starbuck\u2019s body this day week\nmay sink, with all the crew! Great God, where art Thou? Shall I? shall\nI?\u2014The wind has gone down and shifted, sir; the fore and main topsails\nare reefed and set; she heads her course.\u201d\n\n\u201cStern all! Oh Moby Dick, I clutch thy heart at last!\u201d\n\nSuch were the sounds that now came hurtling from out the old man\u2019s\ntormented sleep, as if Starbuck\u2019s voice had caused the long dumb dream\nto speak.\n\nThe yet levelled musket shook like a drunkard\u2019s arm against the panel;\nStarbuck seemed wrestling with an angel; but turning from the door, he\nplaced the death-tube in its rack, and left the place.\n\n\u201cHe\u2019s too sound asleep, Mr. Stubb; go thou down, and wake him, and\ntell him. I must see to the deck here. Thou know\u2019st what to say.\u201d\n\n\n\n\n\nCHAPTER 124. The Needle.\n\nNext morning the not-yet-subsided sea rolled in long slow billows of\nmighty bulk, and striving in the Pequod\u2019s gurgling track, pushed\nher on like giants\u2019 palms outspread. The strong, unstaggering breeze\nabounded so, that sky and air seemed vast outbellying sails; the whole\nworld boomed before the wind. Muffled in the full morning light, the\ninvisible sun was only known by the spread intensity of his place;\nwhere his bayonet rays moved on in stacks. Emblazonings, as of crowned\nBabylonian kings and queens, reigned over everything. The sea was as a\ncrucible of molten gold, that bubblingly leaps with light and heat.\n\nLong maintaining an enchanted silence, Ahab stood apart; and every time\nthe tetering ship loweringly pitched down her bowsprit, he turned to eye\nthe bright sun\u2019s rays produced ahead; and when she profoundly settled\nby the stern, he turned behind, and saw the sun\u2019s rearward place, and\nhow the same yellow rays were blending with his undeviating wake.\n\n\u201cHa, ha, my ship! thou mightest well be taken now for the sea-chariot\nof the sun. Ho, ho! all ye nations before my prow, I bring the sun to\nye! Yoke on the further billows; hallo! a tandem, I drive the sea!\u201d\n\nBut suddenly reined back by some counter thought, he hurried towards the\nhelm, huskily demanding how the ship was heading.\n\n\u201cEast-sou-east, sir,\u201d said the frightened steersman.\n\n\u201cThou liest!\u201d smiting him with his clenched fist. \u201cHeading East at\nthis hour in the morning, and the sun astern?\u201d\n\nUpon this every soul was confounded; for the phenomenon just then\nobserved by Ahab had unaccountably escaped every one else; but its very\nblinding palpableness must have been the cause.\n\nThrusting his head half way into the binnacle, Ahab caught one glimpse\nof the compasses; his uplifted arm slowly fell; for a moment he almost\nseemed to stagger. Standing behind him Starbuck looked, and lo! the two\ncompasses pointed East, and the Pequod was as infallibly going West.\n\nBut ere the first wild alarm could get out abroad among the crew, the\nold man with a rigid laugh exclaimed, \u201cI have it! It has\nhappened before. Mr. Starbuck, last night\u2019s thunder turned our\ncompasses\u2014that\u2019s all. Thou hast before now heard of such a thing, I\ntake it.\u201d\n\n\u201cAye; but never before has it happened to me, sir,\u201d said the pale\nmate, gloomily.\n\nHere, it must needs be said, that accidents like this have in more than\none case occurred to ships in violent storms. The magnetic energy, as\ndeveloped in the mariner\u2019s needle, is, as all know, essentially\none with the electricity beheld in heaven; hence it is not to be much\nmarvelled at, that such things should be. Instances where the lightning\nhas actually struck the vessel, so as to smite down some of the spars\nand rigging, the effect upon the needle has at times been still more\nfatal; all its loadstone virtue being annihilated, so that the before\nmagnetic steel was of no more use than an old wife\u2019s knitting needle.\nBut in either case, the needle never again, of itself, recovers the\noriginal virtue thus marred or lost; and if the binnacle compasses be\naffected, the same fate reaches all the others that may be in the ship;\neven were the lowermost one inserted into the kelson.\n\nDeliberately standing before the binnacle, and eyeing the transpointed\ncompasses, the old man, with the sharp of his extended hand, now took\nthe precise bearing of the sun, and satisfied that the needles were\nexactly inverted, shouted out his orders for the ship\u2019s course to be\nchanged accordingly. The yards were hard up; and once more the Pequod\nthrust her undaunted bows into the opposing wind, for the supposed fair\none had only been juggling her.\n\nMeanwhile, whatever were his own secret thoughts, Starbuck said nothing,\nbut quietly he issued all requisite orders; while Stubb and Flask\u2014who\nin some small degree seemed then to be sharing his feelings\u2014likewise\nunmurmuringly acquiesced. As for the men, though some of them lowly\nrumbled, their fear of Ahab was greater than their fear of Fate. But as\never before, the pagan harpooneers remained almost wholly unimpressed;\nor if impressed, it was only with a certain magnetism shot into their\ncongenial hearts from inflexible Ahab\u2019s.\n\nFor a space the old man walked the deck in rolling reveries. But\nchancing to slip with his ivory heel, he saw the crushed copper\nsight-tubes of the quadrant he had the day before dashed to the deck.\n\n\u201cThou poor, proud heaven-gazer and sun\u2019s pilot! yesterday I wrecked\nthee, and to-day the compasses would fain have wrecked me. So, so.\nBut Ahab is lord over the level loadstone yet. Mr. Starbuck\u2014a lance\nwithout a pole; a top-maul, and the smallest of the sail-maker\u2019s\nneedles. Quick!\u201d\n\nAccessory, perhaps, to the impulse dictating the thing he was now about\nto do, were certain prudential motives, whose object might have been to\nrevive the spirits of his crew by a stroke of his subtile skill, in a\nmatter so wondrous as that of the inverted compasses. Besides, the old\nman well knew that to steer by transpointed needles, though clumsily\npracticable, was not a thing to be passed over by superstitious sailors,\nwithout some shudderings and evil portents.\n\n\u201cMen,\u201d said he, steadily turning upon the crew, as the mate handed\nhim the things he had demanded, \u201cmy men, the thunder turned old\nAhab\u2019s needles; but out of this bit of steel Ahab can make one of his\nown, that will point as true as any.\u201d\n\nAbashed glances of servile wonder were exchanged by the sailors, as this\nwas said; and with fascinated eyes they awaited whatever magic might\nfollow. But Starbuck looked away.\n\nWith a blow from the top-maul Ahab knocked off the steel head of the\nlance, and then handing to the mate the long iron rod remaining, bade\nhim hold it upright, without its touching the deck. Then, with the maul,\nafter repeatedly smiting the upper end of this iron rod, he placed the\nblunted needle endwise on the top of it, and less strongly hammered\nthat, several times, the mate still holding the rod as before. Then\ngoing through some small strange motions with it\u2014whether indispensable\nto the magnetizing of the steel, or merely intended to augment the awe\nof the crew, is uncertain\u2014he called for linen thread; and moving\nto the binnacle, slipped out the two reversed needles there, and\nhorizontally suspended the sail-needle by its middle, over one of the\ncompass-cards. At first, the steel went round and round, quivering and\nvibrating at either end; but at last it settled to its place, when Ahab,\nwho had been intently watching for this result, stepped frankly\nback from the binnacle, and pointing his stretched arm towards it,\nexclaimed,\u2014\u201cLook ye, for yourselves, if Ahab be not lord of the\nlevel loadstone! The sun is East, and that compass swears it!\u201d\n\nOne after another they peered in, for nothing but their own eyes could\npersuade such ignorance as theirs, and one after another they slunk\naway.\n\nIn his fiery eyes of scorn and triumph, you then saw Ahab in all his\nfatal pride.\n\n\n\n\n\nCHAPTER 125. The Log and Line.\n\nWhile now the fated Pequod had been so long afloat this voyage, the log\nand line had but very seldom been in use. Owing to a confident reliance\nupon other means of determining the vessel\u2019s place, some merchantmen,\nand many whalemen, especially when cruising, wholly neglect to heave the\nlog; though at the same time, and frequently more for form\u2019s sake\nthan anything else, regularly putting down upon the customary slate\nthe course steered by the ship, as well as the presumed average rate\nof progression every hour. It had been thus with the Pequod. The wooden\nreel and angular log attached hung, long untouched, just beneath the\nrailing of the after bulwarks. Rains and spray had damped it; sun and\nwind had warped it; all the elements had combined to rot a thing that\nhung so idly. But heedless of all this, his mood seized Ahab, as he\nhappened to glance upon the reel, not many hours after the magnet scene,\nand he remembered how his quadrant was no more, and recalled his frantic\noath about the level log and line. The ship was sailing plungingly;\nastern the billows rolled in riots.\n\n\u201cForward, there! Heave the log!\u201d\n\nTwo seamen came. The golden-hued Tahitian and the grizzly Manxman.\n\u201cTake the reel, one of ye, I\u2019ll heave.\u201d\n\nThey went towards the extreme stern, on the ship\u2019s lee side, where the\ndeck, with the oblique energy of the wind, was now almost dipping into\nthe creamy, sidelong-rushing sea.\n\nThe Manxman took the reel, and holding it high up, by the projecting\nhandle-ends of the spindle, round which the spool of line revolved, so\nstood with the angular log hanging downwards, till Ahab advanced to him.\n\nAhab stood before him, and was lightly unwinding some thirty or forty\nturns to form a preliminary hand-coil to toss overboard, when the old\nManxman, who was intently eyeing both him and the line, made bold to\nspeak.\n\n\u201cSir, I mistrust it; this line looks far gone, long heat and wet have\nspoiled it.\u201d\n\n\u201c\u2018Twill hold, old gentleman. Long heat and wet, have they spoiled\nthee? Thou seem\u2019st to hold. Or, truer perhaps, life holds thee; not\nthou it.\u201d\n\n\u201cI hold the spool, sir. But just as my captain says. With these grey\nhairs of mine \u2018tis not worth while disputing, \u2018specially with a\nsuperior, who\u2019ll ne\u2019er confess.\u201d\n\n\u201cWhat\u2019s that? There now\u2019s a patched professor in Queen Nature\u2019s\ngranite-founded College; but methinks he\u2019s too subservient. Where wert\nthou born?\u201d\n\n\u201cIn the little rocky Isle of Man, sir.\u201d\n\n\u201cExcellent! Thou\u2019st hit the world by that.\u201d\n\n\u201cI know not, sir, but I was born there.\u201d\n\n\u201cIn the Isle of Man, hey? Well, the other way, it\u2019s good. Here\u2019s\na man from Man; a man born in once independent Man, and now unmanned\nof Man; which is sucked in\u2014by what? Up with the reel! The dead, blind\nwall butts all inquiring heads at last. Up with it! So.\u201d\n\nThe log was heaved. The loose coils rapidly straightened out in a long\ndragging line astern, and then, instantly, the reel began to whirl. In\nturn, jerkingly raised and lowered by the rolling billows, the towing\nresistance of the log caused the old reelman to stagger strangely.\n\n\u201cHold hard!\u201d\n\nSnap! the overstrained line sagged down in one long festoon; the tugging\nlog was gone.\n\n\u201cI crush the quadrant, the thunder turns the needles, and now the mad\nsea parts the log-line. But Ahab can mend all. Haul in here, Tahitian;\nreel up, Manxman. And look ye, let the carpenter make another log, and\nmend thou the line. See to it.\u201d\n\n\u201cThere he goes now; to him nothing\u2019s happened; but to me, the\nskewer seems loosening out of the middle of the world. Haul in, haul in,\nTahitian! These lines run whole, and whirling out: come in broken, and\ndragging slow. Ha, Pip? come to help; eh, Pip?\u201d\n\n\u201cPip? whom call ye Pip? Pip jumped from the whale-boat. Pip\u2019s\nmissing. Let\u2019s see now if ye haven\u2019t fished him up here, fisherman.\nIt drags hard; I guess he\u2019s holding on. Jerk him, Tahiti! Jerk him\noff; we haul in no cowards here. Ho! there\u2019s his arm just breaking\nwater. A hatchet! a hatchet! cut it off\u2014we haul in no cowards here.\nCaptain Ahab! sir, sir! here\u2019s Pip, trying to get on board again.\u201d\n\n\u201cPeace, thou crazy loon,\u201d cried the Manxman, seizing him by the arm.\n\u201cAway from the quarter-deck!\u201d\n\n\u201cThe greater idiot ever scolds the lesser,\u201d muttered Ahab,\nadvancing. \u201cHands off from that holiness! Where sayest thou Pip was,\nboy?\n\n\u201cAstern there, sir, astern! Lo! lo!\u201d\n\n\u201cAnd who art thou, boy? I see not my reflection in the vacant pupils\nof thy eyes. Oh God! that man should be a thing for immortal souls to\nsieve through! Who art thou, boy?\u201d\n\n\u201cBell-boy, sir; ship\u2019s-crier; ding, dong, ding! Pip! Pip! Pip!\nOne hundred pounds of clay reward for Pip; five feet high\u2014looks\ncowardly\u2014quickest known by that! Ding, dong, ding! Who\u2019s seen Pip\nthe coward?\u201d\n\n\u201cThere can be no hearts above the snow-line. Oh, ye frozen heavens!\nlook down here. Ye did beget this luckless child, and have abandoned\nhim, ye creative libertines. Here, boy; Ahab\u2019s cabin shall be Pip\u2019s\nhome henceforth, while Ahab lives. Thou touchest my inmost centre, boy;\nthou art tied to me by cords woven of my heart-strings. Come, let\u2019s\ndown.\u201d\n\n\u201cWhat\u2019s this? here\u2019s velvet shark-skin,\u201d intently gazing at\nAhab\u2019s hand, and feeling it. \u201cAh, now, had poor Pip but felt so kind\na thing as this, perhaps he had ne\u2019er been lost! This seems to me,\nsir, as a man-rope; something that weak souls may hold by. Oh, sir, let\nold Perth now come and rivet these two hands together; the black one\nwith the white, for I will not let this go.\u201d\n\n\u201cOh, boy, nor will I thee, unless I should thereby drag thee to worse\nhorrors than are here. Come, then, to my cabin. Lo! ye believers in\ngods all goodness, and in man all ill, lo you! see the omniscient gods\noblivious of suffering man; and man, though idiotic, and knowing not\nwhat he does, yet full of the sweet things of love and gratitude. Come!\nI feel prouder leading thee by thy black hand, than though I grasped an\nEmperor\u2019s!\u201d\n\n\u201cThere go two daft ones now,\u201d muttered the old Manxman. \u201cOne daft\nwith strength, the other daft with weakness. But here\u2019s the end of the\nrotten line\u2014all dripping, too. Mend it, eh? I think we had best have a\nnew line altogether. I\u2019ll see Mr. Stubb about it.\u201d\n\n\n\n\n\nCHAPTER 126. The Life-Buoy.\n\nSteering now south-eastward by Ahab\u2019s levelled steel, and her progress\nsolely determined by Ahab\u2019s level log and line; the Pequod held on\nher path towards the Equator. Making so long a passage through such\nunfrequented waters, descrying no ships, and ere long, sideways impelled\nby unvarying trade winds, over waves monotonously mild; all these seemed\nthe strange calm things preluding some riotous and desperate scene.\n\nAt last, when the ship drew near to the outskirts, as it were, of the\nEquatorial fishing-ground, and in the deep darkness that goes before the\ndawn, was sailing by a cluster of rocky islets; the watch\u2014then\nheaded by Flask\u2014was startled by a cry so plaintively wild and\nunearthly\u2014like half-articulated wailings of the ghosts of all\nHerod\u2019s murdered Innocents\u2014that one and all, they started from their\nreveries, and for the space of some moments stood, or sat, or leaned all\ntransfixedly listening, like the carved Roman slave, while that wild\ncry remained within hearing. The Christian or civilized part of the crew\nsaid it was mermaids, and shuddered; but the pagan harpooneers remained\nunappalled. Yet the grey Manxman\u2014the oldest mariner of all\u2014declared\nthat the wild thrilling sounds that were heard, were the voices of newly\ndrowned men in the sea.\n\nBelow in his hammock, Ahab did not hear of this till grey dawn, when\nhe came to the deck; it was then recounted to him by Flask, not\nunaccompanied with hinted dark meanings. He hollowly laughed, and thus\nexplained the wonder.\n\nThose rocky islands the ship had passed were the resort of great numbers\nof seals, and some young seals that had lost their dams, or some dams\nthat had lost their cubs, must have risen nigh the ship and kept company\nwith her, crying and sobbing with their human sort of wail. But this\nonly the more affected some of them, because most mariners cherish a\nvery superstitious feeling about seals, arising not only from their\npeculiar tones when in distress, but also from the human look of their\nround heads and semi-intelligent faces, seen peeringly uprising from\nthe water alongside. In the sea, under certain circumstances, seals have\nmore than once been mistaken for men.\n\nBut the bodings of the crew were destined to receive a most plausible\nconfirmation in the fate of one of their number that morning. At\nsun-rise this man went from his hammock to his mast-head at the fore;\nand whether it was that he was not yet half waked from his sleep (for\nsailors sometimes go aloft in a transition state), whether it was thus\nwith the man, there is now no telling; but, be that as it may, he\nhad not been long at his perch, when a cry was heard\u2014a cry and a\nrushing\u2014and looking up, they saw a falling phantom in the air; and\nlooking down, a little tossed heap of white bubbles in the blue of the\nsea.\n\nThe life-buoy\u2014a long slender cask\u2014was dropped from the stern, where\nit always hung obedient to a cunning spring; but no hand rose to seize\nit, and the sun having long beat upon this cask it had shrunken, so that\nit slowly filled, and that parched wood also filled at its every pore;\nand the studded iron-bound cask followed the sailor to the bottom, as if\nto yield him his pillow, though in sooth but a hard one.\n\nAnd thus the first man of the Pequod that mounted the mast to look out\nfor the White Whale, on the White Whale\u2019s own peculiar ground; that\nman was swallowed up in the deep. But few, perhaps, thought of that at\nthe time. Indeed, in some sort, they were not grieved at this event, at\nleast as a portent; for they regarded it, not as a foreshadowing of evil\nin the future, but as the fulfilment of an evil already presaged. They\ndeclared that now they knew the reason of those wild shrieks they had\nheard the night before. But again the old Manxman said nay.\n\nThe lost life-buoy was now to be replaced; Starbuck was directed to see\nto it; but as no cask of sufficient lightness could be found, and as\nin the feverish eagerness of what seemed the approaching crisis of\nthe voyage, all hands were impatient of any toil but what was directly\nconnected with its final end, whatever that might prove to be;\ntherefore, they were going to leave the ship\u2019s stern unprovided with a\nbuoy, when by certain strange signs and inuendoes Queequeg hinted a hint\nconcerning his coffin.\n\n\u201cA life-buoy of a coffin!\u201d cried Starbuck, starting.\n\n\u201cRather queer, that, I should say,\u201d said Stubb.\n\n\u201cIt will make a good enough one,\u201d said Flask, \u201cthe carpenter here\ncan arrange it easily.\u201d\n\n\u201cBring it up; there\u2019s nothing else for it,\u201d said Starbuck, after\na melancholy pause. \u201cRig it, carpenter; do not look at me so\u2014the\ncoffin, I mean. Dost thou hear me? Rig it.\u201d\n\n\u201cAnd shall I nail down the lid, sir?\u201d moving his hand as with a\nhammer.\n\n\u201cAye.\u201d\n\n\u201cAnd shall I caulk the seams, sir?\u201d moving his hand as with a\ncaulking-iron.\n\n\u201cAye.\u201d\n\n\u201cAnd shall I then pay over the same with pitch, sir?\u201d moving his\nhand as with a pitch-pot.\n\n\u201cAway! what possesses thee to this? Make a life-buoy of the coffin,\nand no more.\u2014Mr. Stubb, Mr. Flask, come forward with me.\u201d\n\n\u201cHe goes off in a huff. The whole he can endure; at the parts he\nbaulks. Now I don\u2019t like this. I make a leg for Captain Ahab, and he\nwears it like a gentleman; but I make a bandbox for Queequeg, and he\nwon\u2019t put his head into it. Are all my pains to go for nothing with\nthat coffin? And now I\u2019m ordered to make a life-buoy of it. It\u2019s\nlike turning an old coat; going to bring the flesh on the other side\nnow. I don\u2019t like this cobbling sort of business\u2014I don\u2019t like it\nat all; it\u2019s undignified; it\u2019s not my place. Let tinkers\u2019 brats do\ntinkerings; we are their betters. I like to take in hand none but clean,\nvirgin, fair-and-square mathematical jobs, something that regularly\nbegins at the beginning, and is at the middle when midway, and comes to\nan end at the conclusion; not a cobbler\u2019s job, that\u2019s at an end in\nthe middle, and at the beginning at the end. It\u2019s the old woman\u2019s\ntricks to be giving cobbling jobs. Lord! what an affection all old women\nhave for tinkers. I know an old woman of sixty-five who ran away with\na bald-headed young tinker once. And that\u2019s the reason I never would\nwork for lonely widow old women ashore, when I kept my job-shop in the\nVineyard; they might have taken it into their lonely old heads to run\noff with me. But heigh-ho! there are no caps at sea but snow-caps.\nLet me see. Nail down the lid; caulk the seams; pay over the same with\npitch; batten them down tight, and hang it with the snap-spring over the\nship\u2019s stern. Were ever such things done before with a coffin? Some\nsuperstitious old carpenters, now, would be tied up in the rigging, ere\nthey would do the job. But I\u2019m made of knotty Aroostook hemlock; I\ndon\u2019t budge. Cruppered with a coffin! Sailing about with a grave-yard\ntray! But never mind. We workers in woods make bridal-bedsteads and\ncard-tables, as well as coffins and hearses. We work by the month, or\nby the job, or by the profit; not for us to ask the why and wherefore of\nour work, unless it be too confounded cobbling, and then we stash it if\nwe can. Hem! I\u2019ll do the job, now, tenderly. I\u2019ll have me\u2014let\u2019s\nsee\u2014how many in the ship\u2019s company, all told? But I\u2019ve forgotten.\nAny way, I\u2019ll have me thirty separate, Turk\u2019s-headed life-lines,\neach three feet long hanging all round to the coffin. Then, if the\nhull go down, there\u2019ll be thirty lively fellows all fighting for\none coffin, a sight not seen very often beneath the sun! Come hammer,\ncaulking-iron, pitch-pot, and marling-spike! Let\u2019s to it.\u201d\n\n\n\n\n\nCHAPTER 127. The Deck.\n\nThe coffin laid upon two line-tubs, between the vice-bench and the open\nhatchway; the Carpenter caulking its seams; the string of twisted oakum\nslowly unwinding from a large roll of it placed in the bosom of his\nfrock.\u2014Ahab comes slowly from the cabin-gangway, and hears Pip\nfollowing him.\n\n\u201cBack, lad; I will be with ye again presently. He goes! Not this hand\ncomplies with my humor more genially than that boy.\u2014Middle aisle of a\nchurch! What\u2019s here?\u201d\n\n\u201cLife-buoy, sir. Mr. Starbuck\u2019s orders. Oh, look, sir! Beware the\nhatchway!\u201d\n\n\u201cThank ye, man. Thy coffin lies handy to the vault.\u201d\n\n\u201cSir? The hatchway? oh! So it does, sir, so it does.\u201d\n\n\u201cArt not thou the leg-maker? Look, did not this stump come from thy\nshop?\u201d\n\n\u201cI believe it did, sir; does the ferrule stand, sir?\u201d\n\n\u201cWell enough. But art thou not also the undertaker?\u201d\n\n\u201cAye, sir; I patched up this thing here as a coffin for Queequeg; but\nthey\u2019ve set me now to turning it into something else.\u201d\n\n\u201cThen tell me; art thou not an arrant, all-grasping, intermeddling,\nmonopolising, heathenish old scamp, to be one day making legs, and the\nnext day coffins to clap them in, and yet again life-buoys out of those\nsame coffins? Thou art as unprincipled as the gods, and as much of a\njack-of-all-trades.\u201d\n\n\u201cBut I do not mean anything, sir. I do as I do.\u201d\n\n\u201cThe gods again. Hark ye, dost thou not ever sing working about a\ncoffin? The Titans, they say, hummed snatches when chipping out the\ncraters for volcanoes; and the grave-digger in the play sings, spade in\nhand. Dost thou never?\u201d\n\n\u201cSing, sir? Do I sing? Oh, I\u2019m indifferent enough, sir, for that;\nbut the reason why the grave-digger made music must have been because\nthere was none in his spade, sir. But the caulking mallet is full of it.\nHark to it.\u201d\n\n\u201cAye, and that\u2019s because the lid there\u2019s a sounding-board; and\nwhat in all things makes the sounding-board is this\u2014there\u2019s naught\nbeneath. And yet, a coffin with a body in it rings pretty much the same,\nCarpenter. Hast thou ever helped carry a bier, and heard the coffin\nknock against the churchyard gate, going in?\n\n\u201cFaith, sir, I\u2019ve\u2014\u201d\n\n\u201cFaith? What\u2019s that?\u201d\n\n\u201cWhy, faith, sir, it\u2019s only a sort of exclamation-like\u2014that\u2019s\nall, sir.\u201d\n\n\u201cUm, um; go on.\u201d\n\n\u201cI was about to say, sir, that\u2014\u201d\n\n\u201cArt thou a silk-worm? Dost thou spin thy own shroud out of thyself?\nLook at thy bosom! Despatch! and get these traps out of sight.\u201d\n\n\u201cHe goes aft. That was sudden, now; but squalls come sudden in\nhot latitudes. I\u2019ve heard that the Isle of Albemarle, one of the\nGallipagos, is cut by the Equator right in the middle. Seems to me\nsome sort of Equator cuts yon old man, too, right in his middle. He\u2019s\nalways under the Line\u2014fiery hot, I tell ye! He\u2019s looking this\nway\u2014come, oakum; quick. Here we go again. This wooden mallet is the\ncork, and I\u2019m the professor of musical glasses\u2014tap, tap!\u201d\n\n(Ahab to himself.)\n\n\u201cThere\u2019s a sight! There\u2019s a sound! The grey-headed woodpecker\ntapping the hollow tree! Blind and dumb might well be envied now. See!\nthat thing rests on two line-tubs, full of tow-lines. A most malicious\nwag, that fellow. Rat-tat! So man\u2019s seconds tick! Oh! how immaterial\nare all materials! What things real are there, but imponderable\nthoughts? Here now\u2019s the very dreaded symbol of grim death, by a mere\nhap, made the expressive sign of the help and hope of most endangered\nlife. A life-buoy of a coffin! Does it go further? Can it be that\nin some spiritual sense the coffin is, after all, but an\nimmortality-preserver! I\u2019ll think of that. But no. So far gone am I in\nthe dark side of earth, that its other side, the theoretic bright one,\nseems but uncertain twilight to me. Will ye never have done, Carpenter,\nwith that accursed sound? I go below; let me not see that thing here\nwhen I return again. Now, then, Pip, we\u2019ll talk this over; I do suck\nmost wondrous philosophies from thee! Some unknown conduits from the\nunknown worlds must empty into thee!\u201d\n\n\n\n\n\nCHAPTER 128. The Pequod Meets The Rachel.\n\nNext day, a large ship, the Rachel, was descried, bearing directly down\nupon the Pequod, all her spars thickly clustering with men. At the\ntime the Pequod was making good speed through the water; but as the\nbroad-winged windward stranger shot nigh to her, the boastful sails all\nfell together as blank bladders that are burst, and all life fled from\nthe smitten hull.\n\n\u201cBad news; she brings bad news,\u201d muttered the old Manxman. But ere\nher commander, who, with trumpet to mouth, stood up in his boat; ere he\ncould hopefully hail, Ahab\u2019s voice was heard.\n\n\u201cHast seen the White Whale?\u201d\n\n\u201cAye, yesterday. Have ye seen a whale-boat adrift?\u201d\n\nThrottling his joy, Ahab negatively answered this unexpected question;\nand would then have fain boarded the stranger, when the stranger captain\nhimself, having stopped his vessel\u2019s way, was seen descending her\nside. A few keen pulls, and his boat-hook soon clinched the Pequod\u2019s\nmain-chains, and he sprang to the deck. Immediately he was recognised by\nAhab for a Nantucketer he knew. But no formal salutation was exchanged.\n\n\u201cWhere was he?\u2014not killed!\u2014not killed!\u201d cried Ahab, closely\nadvancing. \u201cHow was it?\u201d\n\nIt seemed that somewhat late on the afternoon of the day previous, while\nthree of the stranger\u2019s boats were engaged with a shoal of whales,\nwhich had led them some four or five miles from the ship; and while they\nwere yet in swift chase to windward, the white hump and head of Moby\nDick had suddenly loomed up out of the water, not very far to leeward;\nwhereupon, the fourth rigged boat\u2014a reserved one\u2014had been instantly\nlowered in chase. After a keen sail before the wind, this fourth\nboat\u2014the swiftest keeled of all\u2014seemed to have succeeded in\nfastening\u2014at least, as well as the man at the mast-head could tell\nanything about it. In the distance he saw the diminished dotted boat;\nand then a swift gleam of bubbling white water; and after that nothing\nmore; whence it was concluded that the stricken whale must have\nindefinitely run away with his pursuers, as often happens. There was\nsome apprehension, but no positive alarm, as yet. The recall signals\nwere placed in the rigging; darkness came on; and forced to pick up her\nthree far to windward boats\u2014ere going in quest of the fourth one\nin the precisely opposite direction\u2014the ship had not only been\nnecessitated to leave that boat to its fate till near midnight, but,\nfor the time, to increase her distance from it. But the rest of her\ncrew being at last safe aboard, she crowded all sail\u2014stunsail on\nstunsail\u2014after the missing boat; kindling a fire in her try-pots for\na beacon; and every other man aloft on the look-out. But though when she\nhad thus sailed a sufficient distance to gain the presumed place of the\nabsent ones when last seen; though she then paused to lower her spare\nboats to pull all around her; and not finding anything, had again\ndashed on; again paused, and lowered her boats; and though she had thus\ncontinued doing till daylight; yet not the least glimpse of the missing\nkeel had been seen.\n\nThe story told, the stranger Captain immediately went on to reveal his\nobject in boarding the Pequod. He desired that ship to unite with his\nown in the search; by sailing over the sea some four or five miles\napart, on parallel lines, and so sweeping a double horizon, as it were.\n\n\u201cI will wager something now,\u201d whispered Stubb to Flask, \u201cthat some\none in that missing boat wore off that Captain\u2019s best coat; mayhap,\nhis watch\u2014he\u2019s so cursed anxious to get it back. Who ever heard\nof two pious whale-ships cruising after one missing whale-boat in\nthe height of the whaling season? See, Flask, only see how pale he\nlooks\u2014pale in the very buttons of his eyes\u2014look\u2014it wasn\u2019t the\ncoat\u2014it must have been the\u2014\u201d\n\n\u201cMy boy, my own boy is among them.
