We must save that boy.\u201d\n\n\u201cHe\u2019s drowned with the rest on \u2018em, last night,\u201d said the old\nManx sailor standing behind them; \u201cI heard; all of ye heard their\nspirits.\u201d\n\nNow, as it shortly turned out, what made this incident of the Rachel\u2019s\nthe more melancholy, was the circumstance, that not only was one of\nthe Captain\u2019s sons among the number of the missing boat\u2019s crew; but\namong the number of the other boat\u2019s crews, at the same time, but on\nthe other hand, separated from the ship during the dark vicissitudes\nof the chase, there had been still another son; as that for a time, the\nwretched father was plunged to the bottom of the cruellest perplexity;\nwhich was only solved for him by his chief mate\u2019s instinctively\nadopting the ordinary procedure of a whale-ship in such emergencies,\nthat is, when placed between jeopardized but divided boats, always\nto pick up the majority first. But the captain, for some unknown\nconstitutional reason, had refrained from mentioning all this, and\nnot till forced to it by Ahab\u2019s iciness did he allude to his one yet\nmissing boy; a little lad, but twelve years old, whose father with the\nearnest but unmisgiving hardihood of a Nantucketer\u2019s paternal love,\nhad thus early sought to initiate him in the perils and wonders of a\nvocation almost immemorially the destiny of all his race. Nor does it\nunfrequently occur, that Nantucket captains will send a son of such\ntender age away from them, for a protracted three or four years\u2019\nvoyage in some other ship than their own; so that their first knowledge\nof a whaleman\u2019s career shall be unenervated by any chance display of\na father\u2019s natural but untimely partiality, or undue apprehensiveness\nand concern.\n\nMeantime, now the stranger was still beseeching his poor boon of Ahab;\nand Ahab still stood like an anvil, receiving every shock, but without\nthe least quivering of his own.\n\n\u201cI will not go,\u201d said the stranger, \u201ctill you say aye to me. Mr. Starbuck, look at the binnacle\nwatch, and in three minutes from this present instant warn off all\nstrangers: then brace forward again, and let the ship sail as before.\u201d\n\nHurriedly turning, with averted face, he descended into his cabin,\nleaving the strange captain transfixed at this unconditional and utter\nrejection of his so earnest suit. But starting from his enchantment,\nGardiner silently hurried to the side; more fell than stepped into his\nboat, and returned to his ship.\n\nSoon the two ships diverged their wakes; and long as the strange vessel\nwas in view, she was seen to yaw hither and thither at every dark spot,\nhowever small, on the sea. This way and that her yards were swung round;\nstarboard and larboard, she continued to tack; now she beat against a\nhead sea; and again it pushed her before it; while all the while, her\nmasts and yards were thickly clustered with men, as three tall cherry\ntrees, when the boys are cherrying among the boughs.\n\nBut by her still halting course and winding, woeful way, you plainly saw\nthat this ship that so wept with spray, still remained without comfort.\nShe was Rachel, weeping for her children, because they were not.\n\n\n\n\n\nCHAPTER 129. The Cabin.\n\n(Ahab moving to go on deck; Pip catches him by the hand to follow.)\n\n\u201cLad, lad, I tell thee thou must not follow Ahab now. The Hat.\n\nAnd now that at the proper time and place, after so long and wide a\npreliminary cruise, Ahab,\u2014all other whaling waters swept\u2014seemed to\nhave chased his foe into an ocean-fold, to slay him the more securely\nthere; now, that he found himself hard by the very latitude and\nlongitude where his tormenting wound had been inflicted; now that a\nvessel had been spoken which on the very day preceding had actually\nencountered Moby Dick;\u2014and now that all his successive meetings with\nvarious ships contrastingly concurred to show the demoniac indifference\nwith which the white whale tore his hunters, whether sinning or sinned\nagainst; now it was that there lurked a something in the old man\u2019s\neyes, which it was hardly sufferable for feeble souls to see. As the\nunsetting polar star, which through the livelong, arctic, six months\u2019\nnight sustains its piercing, steady, central gaze; so Ahab\u2019s purpose\nnow fixedly gleamed down upon the constant midnight of the gloomy crew.\nIt domineered above them so, that all their bodings, doubts, misgivings,\nfears, were fain to hide beneath their souls, and not sprout forth a\nsingle spear or leaf.\n\nIn this foreshadowing interval too, all humor, forced or natural,\nvanished. Stubb no more strove to raise a smile; Starbuck no more strove\nto check one. Alike, joy and sorrow, hope and fear, seemed ground\nto finest dust, and powdered, for the time, in the clamped mortar of\nAhab\u2019s iron soul. Like machines, they dumbly moved about the deck,\never conscious that the old man\u2019s despot eye was on them.\n\nBut did you deeply scan him in his more secret confidential hours; when\nhe thought no glance but one was on him; then you would have seen that\neven as Ahab\u2019s eyes so awed the crew\u2019s, the inscrutable Parsee\u2019s\nglance awed his; or somehow, at least, in some wild way, at times\naffected it. Such an added, gliding strangeness began to invest the thin\nFedallah now; such ceaseless shudderings shook him; that the men looked\ndubious at him; half uncertain, as it seemed, whether indeed he were a\nmortal substance, or else a tremulous shadow cast upon the deck by some\nunseen being\u2019s body. And that shadow was always hovering there. For\nnot by night, even, had Fedallah ever certainly been known to slumber,\nor go below. He would stand still for hours: but never sat or leaned;\nhis wan but wondrous eyes did plainly say\u2014We two watchmen never rest.\n\nNor, at any time, by night or day could the mariners now step upon the\ndeck, unless Ahab was before them; either standing in his pivot-hole,\nor exactly pacing the planks between two undeviating limits,\u2014the\nmain-mast and the mizen; or else they saw him standing in the\ncabin-scuttle,\u2014his living foot advanced upon the deck, as if to step;\nhis hat slouched heavily over his eyes; so that however motionless he\nstood, however the days and nights were added on, that he had not swung\nin his hammock; yet hidden beneath that slouching hat, they could never\ntell unerringly whether, for all this, his eyes were really closed at\ntimes; or whether he was still intently scanning them; no matter, though\nhe stood so in the scuttle for a whole hour on the stretch, and the\nunheeded night-damp gathered in beads of dew upon that stone-carved coat\nand hat. The clothes that the night had wet, the next day\u2019s sunshine\ndried upon him; and so, day after day, and night after night; he went no\nmore beneath the planks; whatever he wanted from the cabin that thing he\nsent for.\n\nHe ate in the same open air; that is, his two only meals,\u2014breakfast\nand dinner: supper he never touched; nor reaped his beard; which darkly\ngrew all gnarled, as unearthed roots of trees blown over, which still\ngrow idly on at naked base, though perished in the upper verdure. But\nthough his whole life was now become one watch on deck; and though the\nParsee\u2019s mystic watch was without intermission as his own; yet these\ntwo never seemed to speak\u2014one man to the other\u2014unless at long\nintervals some passing unmomentous matter made it necessary. Though such\na potent spell seemed secretly to join the twain; openly, and to the\nawe-struck crew, they seemed pole-like asunder. If by day they chanced\nto speak one word; by night, dumb men were both, so far as concerned\nthe slightest verbal interchange. At times, for longest hours, without\na single hail, they stood far parted in the starlight; Ahab in his\nscuttle, the Parsee by the mainmast; but still fixedly gazing upon each\nother; as if in the Parsee Ahab saw his forethrown shadow, in Ahab the\nParsee his abandoned substance.\n\nAnd yet, somehow, did Ahab\u2014in his own proper self, as daily, hourly,\nand every instant, commandingly revealed to his subordinates,\u2014Ahab\nseemed an independent lord; the Parsee but his slave. And thus, with one hand clinging round the\nroyal mast, Ahab gazed abroad upon the sea for miles and miles,\u2014ahead,\nastern, this side, and that,\u2014within the wide expanded circle commanded\nat so great a height.\n\nWhen in working with his hands at some lofty almost isolated place in\nthe rigging, which chances to afford no foothold, the sailor at sea is\nhoisted up to that spot, and sustained there by the rope; under these\ncircumstances, its fastened end on deck is always given in strict charge\nto some one man who has the special watch of it. Because in such a\nwilderness of running rigging, whose various different relations aloft\ncannot always be infallibly discerned by what is seen of them at the\ndeck; and when the deck-ends of these ropes are being every few minutes\ncast down from the fastenings, it would be but a natural fatality, if,\nunprovided with a constant watchman, the hoisted sailor should by some\ncarelessness of the crew be cast adrift and fall all swooping to the\nsea. But only by the replacing of the cap was that omen\naccounted good. Ahab\u2019s hat was never restored; the wild hawk flew on\nand on with it; far in advance of the prow: and at last disappeared;\nwhile from the point of that disappearance, a minute black spot was\ndimly discerned, falling from that vast height into the sea.\n\n\n\n\n\nCHAPTER 131. The Pequod Meets The Delight.\n\nThe intense Pequod sailed on; the rolling waves and days went by; the\nlife-buoy-coffin still lightly swung; and another ship, most miserably\nmisnamed the Delight, was descried. As she drew nigh, all eyes were\nfixed upon her broad beams, called shears, which, in some whaling-ships,\ncross the quarter-deck at the height of eight or nine feet; serving to\ncarry the spare, unrigged, or disabled boats.\n\nUpon the stranger\u2019s shears were beheld the shattered, white ribs, and\nsome few splintered planks, of what had once been a whale-boat; but you\nnow saw through this wreck, as plainly as you see through the peeled,\nhalf-unhinged, and bleaching skeleton of a horse.\n\n\u201cHast seen the White Whale?\u201d\n\n\u201cLook!\u201d replied the hollow-cheeked captain from his taffrail; and\nwith his trumpet he pointed to the wreck.\n\n\u201cHast killed him?\u201d\n\n\u201cThe harpoon is not yet forged that ever will do that,\u201d answered the\nother, sadly glancing upon a rounded hammock on the deck, whose gathered\nsides some noiseless sailors were busy in sewing together.\n\n\u201cNot forged!\u201d and snatching Perth\u2019s levelled iron from the crotch,\nAhab held it out, exclaiming\u2014\u201cLook ye, Nantucketer; here in this\nhand I hold his death! The Symphony.\n\nIt was a clear steel-blue day. The firmaments of air and sea were\nhardly separable in that all-pervading azure; only, the pensive air was\ntransparently pure and soft, with a woman\u2019s look, and the robust and\nman-like sea heaved with long, strong, lingering swells, as Samson\u2019s\nchest in his sleep.\n\nHither, and thither, on high, glided the snow-white wings of small,\nunspeckled birds; these were the gentle thoughts of the feminine air;\nbut to and fro in the deeps, far down in the bottomless blue, rushed\nmighty leviathans, sword-fish, and sharks; and these were the strong,\ntroubled, murderous thinkings of the masculine sea.\n\nBut though thus contrasting within, the contrast was only in shades and\nshadows without; those two seemed one; it was only the sex, as it were,\nthat distinguished them.\n\nAloft, like a royal czar and king, the sun seemed giving this gentle\nair to this bold and rolling sea; even as bride to groom. And at the\ngirdling line of the horizon, a soft and tremulous motion\u2014most seen\nhere at the Equator\u2014denoted the fond, throbbing trust, the loving\nalarms, with which the poor bride gave her bosom away.\n\nTied up and twisted; gnarled and knotted with wrinkles; haggardly firm\nand unyielding; his eyes glowing like coals, that still glow in the\nashes of ruin; untottering Ahab stood forth in the clearness of the\nmorn; lifting his splintered helmet of a brow to the fair girl\u2019s\nforehead of heaven.\n\nOh, immortal infancy, and innocency of the azure! Invisible winged\ncreatures that frolic all round us! Sweet childhood of air and sky! how\noblivious were ye of old Ahab\u2019s close-coiled woe! But so have I seen\nlittle Miriam and Martha, laughing-eyed elves, heedlessly gambol around\ntheir old sire; sporting with the circle of singed locks which grew on\nthe marge of that burnt-out crater of his brain.\n\nSlowly crossing the deck from the scuttle, Ahab leaned over the side and\nwatched how his shadow in the water sank and sank to his gaze, the more\nand the more that he strove to pierce the profundity. But the lovely\naromas in that enchanted air did at last seem to dispel, for a moment,\nthe cankerous thing in his soul. That glad, happy air, that winsome\nsky, did at last stroke and caress him; the step-mother world, so long\ncruel\u2014forbidding\u2014now threw affectionate arms round his stubborn\nneck, and did seem to joyously sob over him, as if over one, that\nhowever wilful and erring, she could yet find it in her heart to save\nand to bless. From beneath his slouched hat Ahab dropped a tear into the\nsea; nor did all the Pacific contain such wealth as that one wee drop.\n\nStarbuck saw the old man; saw him, how he heavily leaned over the side;\nand he seemed to hear in his own true heart the measureless sobbing that\nstole out of the centre of the serenity around. Careful not to touch\nhim, or be noticed by him, he yet drew near to him, and stood there.\n\nAhab turned.\n\n\u201cStarbuck!\u201d\n\n\u201cSir.\u201d\n\n\u201cOh, Starbuck! it is a mild, mild wind, and a mild looking sky. On\nsuch a day\u2014very much such a sweetness as this\u2014I struck my first\nwhale\u2014a boy-harpooneer of eighteen! Forty\u2014forty\u2014forty years\nago!\u2014ago! Forty years of continual whaling! forty years of privation,\nand peril, and storm-time! forty years on the pitiless sea! for forty\nyears has Ahab forsaken the peaceful land, for forty years to make war\non the horrors of the deep! Aye and yes, Starbuck, out of those forty\nyears I have not spent three ashore. When I think of this life I have\nled; the desolation of solitude it has been; the masoned, walled-town\nof a Captain\u2019s exclusiveness, which admits but small entrance to any\nsympathy from the green country without\u2014oh, weariness! heaviness!\nGuinea-coast slavery of solitary command!\u2014when I think of all this;\nonly half-suspected, not so keenly known to me before\u2014and how for\nforty years I have fed upon dry salted fare\u2014fit emblem of the dry\nnourishment of my soil!\u2014when the poorest landsman has had fresh fruit\nto his daily hand, and broken the world\u2019s fresh bread to my mouldy\ncrusts\u2014away, whole oceans away, from that young girl-wife I wedded\npast fifty, and sailed for Cape Horn the next day, leaving but one dent\nin my marriage pillow\u2014wife? wife?\u2014rather a widow with her husband\nalive!
