Well, in that hill is all the treasures\nof the earth, and I was looking around for a man with a particular good\nkind heart and a noble, generous disposition, because if I could find\njust that man, I've got a kind of a salve I could put on his eyes and he\ncould see the treasures and get them out.\"\n\nSo then the camel-driver was in a sweat; and he cried, and begged, and\ntook on, and went down on his knees, and said he was just that kind of a\nman, and said he could fetch a thousand people that would say he wasn't\never described so exact before.\n\n\"Well, then,\" says the dervish, \"all right. If we load the hundred\ncamels, can I have half of them?\"\n\nThe driver was so glad he couldn't hardly hold in, and says:\n\n\"Now you're shouting.\"\n\nSo they shook hands on the bargain, and the dervish got out his box and\nrubbed the salve on the driver's right eye, and the hill opened and he\nwent in, and there, sure enough, was piles and piles of gold and jewels\nsparkling like all the stars in heaven had fell down.\n\nSo him and the dervish laid into it, and they loaded every camel till\nhe couldn't carry no more; then they said good-bye, and each of them\nstarted off with his fifty. But pretty soon the camel-driver come\na-running and overtook the dervish and says:\n\n\"You ain't in society, you know, and you don't really need all you've\ngot. Won't you be good, and let me have ten of your camels?\"\n\n\"Well,\" the dervish says, \"I don't know but what you say is reasonable\nenough.\"\n\nSo he done it, and they separated and the dervish started off again with\nhis forty. But pretty soon here comes the camel-driver bawling after him\nagain, and whines and slobbers around and begs another ten off of him,\nsaying thirty camel loads of treasures was enough to see a dervish\nthrough, because they live very simple, you know, and don't keep house,\nbut board around and give their note.\n\nBut that warn't the end yet. That ornery hound kept coming and coming\ntill he had begged back all the camels and had the whole hundred. Then\nhe was satisfied, and ever so grateful, and said he wouldn't ever forgit\nthe dervish as long as he lived, and nobody hadn't been so good to him\nbefore, and liberal. So they shook hands good-bye, and separated and\nstarted off again.\n\nBut do you know, it warn't ten minutes till the camel-driver was\nunsatisfied again--he was the lowdownest reptyle in seven counties--and\nhe come a-running again. And this time the thing he wanted was to get\nthe dervish to rub some of the salve on his other eye.\n\n\"Why?\" said the dervish.\n\n\"Oh, you know,\" says the driver.\n\n\"Know what?\"\n\n\"Well, you can't fool me,\" says the driver. \"You're trying to keep back\nsomething from me, you know it mighty well. You know, I reckon, that if\nI had the salve on the other eye I could see a lot more things that's\nvaluable. Come--please put it on.\"\n\nThe dervish says:\n\n\"I wasn't keeping anything back from you. I don't mind telling you what\nwould happen if I put it on. You'd never see again. You'd be stone-blind\nthe rest of your days.\"\n\nBut do you know that beat wouldn't believe him. No, he begged and\nbegged, and whined and cried, till at last the dervish opened his box\nand told him to put it on, if he wanted to. So the man done it, and sure\nenough he was as blind as a bat in a minute.\n\nThen the dervish laughed at him and mocked at him and made fun of him;\nand says:\n\n\"Good-bye--a man that's blind hain't got no use for jewelry.\"\n\nAnd he cleared out with the hundred camels, and left that man to wander\naround poor and miserable and friendless the rest of his days in the\nDesert.\n\nJim said he'd bet it was a lesson to him.\n\n\"Yes,\" Tom says, \"and like a considerable many lessons a body gets.\nThey ain't no account, because the thing don't ever happen the same way\nagain--and can't. The time Hen Scovil fell down the chimbly and crippled\nhis back for life, everybody said it would be a lesson to him. What kind\nof a lesson? How was he going to use it? He couldn't climb chimblies no\nmore, and he hadn't no more backs to break.\"\n\n\"All de same, Mars Tom, dey IS sich a thing as learnin' by expe'ence. De\nGood Book say de burnt chile shun de fire.\"\n\n\"Well, I ain't denying that a thing's a lesson if it's a thing that can\nhappen twice just the same way. There's lots of such things, and THEY\neducate a person, that's what Uncle Abner always said; but there's forty\nMILLION lots of the other kind--the kind that don't happen the same way\ntwice--and they ain't no real use, they ain't no more instructive than\nthe small-pox. When you've got it, it ain't no good to find out you\nought to been vaccinated, and it ain't no good to git vaccinated\nafterward, because the small-pox don't come but once. But, on the other\nhand, Uncle Abner said that the person that had took a bull by the tail\nonce had learnt sixty or seventy times as much as a person that hadn't,\nand said a person that started in to carry a cat home by the tail was\ngitting knowledge that was always going to be useful to him, and warn't\never going to grow dim or doubtful. But I can tell you, Jim, Uncle Abner\nwas down on them people that's all the time trying to dig a lesson out\nof everything that happens, no matter whether--\"\n\nBut Jim was asleep. Tom looked kind of ashamed, because you know a\nperson always feels bad when he is talking uncommon fine and thinks the\nother person is admiring, and that other person goes to sleep that way.\nOf course he oughtn't to go to sleep, because it's shabby; but the finer\na person talks the certainer it is to make you sleep, and so when you\ncome to look at it it ain't nobody's fault in particular; both of them's\nto blame.\n\nJim begun to snore--soft and blubbery at first, then a long rasp, then\na stronger one, then a half a dozen horrible ones like the last water\nsucking down the plug-hole of a bath-tub, then the same with more power\nto it, and some big coughs and snorts flung in, the way a cow does that\nis choking to death; and when the person has got to that point he is at\nhis level best, and can wake up a man that is in the next block with\na dipperful of loddanum in him, but can't wake himself up although all\nthat awful noise of his'n ain't but three inches from his own ears. And\nthat is the curiosest thing in the world, seems to me. But you rake a\nmatch to light the candle, and that little bit of a noise will fetch\nhim. I wish I knowed what was the reason of that, but there don't seem\nto be no way to find out. Now there was Jim alarming the whole Desert,\nand yanking the animals out, for miles and miles around, to see what in\nthe nation was going on up there; there warn't nobody nor nothing that\nwas as close to the noise as HE was, and yet he was the only cretur that\nwasn't disturbed by it. We yelled at him and whooped at him, it never\ndone no good; but the first time there come a little wee noise that\nwasn't of a usual kind it woke him up. No, sir, I've thought it all\nover, and so has Tom, and there ain't no way to find out why a snorer\ncan't hear himself snore.\n\nJim said he hadn't been asleep; he just shut his eyes so he could listen\nbetter.\n\nTom said nobody warn't accusing him.\n\nThat made him look like he wished he hadn't said anything. And he wanted\nto git away from the subject, I reckon, because he begun to abuse the\ncamel-driver, just the way a person does when he has got catched in\nsomething and wants to take it out of somebody else. He let into the\ncamel-driver the hardest he knowed how, and I had to agree with him; and\nhe praised up the dervish the highest he could, and I had to agree with\nhim there, too. But Tom says:\n\n\"I ain't so sure. You call that dervish so dreadful liberal and good\nand unselfish, but I don't quite see it. He didn't hunt up another poor\ndervish, did he? No, he didn't. If he was so unselfish, why didn't he\ngo in there himself and take a pocketful of jewels and go along and\nbe satisfied? No, sir, the person he was hunting for was a man with a\nhundred camels. He wanted to get away with all the treasure he could.\"\n\n\"Why, Mars Tom, he was willin' to divide, fair and square; he only\nstruck for fifty camels.\"\n\n\"Because he knowed how he was going to get all of them by and by.\"\n\n\"Mars Tom, he TOLE de man de truck would make him bline.\"\n\n\"Yes, because he knowed the man's character. It was just the kind of a\nman he was hunting for--a man that never believes in anybody's word or\nanybody's honorableness, because he ain't got none of his own. I reckon\nthere's lots of people like that dervish. They swindle, right and left,\nbut they always make the other person SEEM to swindle himself. They keep\ninside of the letter of the law all the time, and there ain't no way\nto git hold of them. THEY don't put the salve on--oh, no, that would\nbe sin; but they know how to fool YOU into putting it on, then it's you\nthat blinds yourself. I reckon the dervish and the camel-driver was just\na pair--a fine, smart, brainy rascal, and a dull, coarse, ignorant one,\nbut both of them rascals, just the same.\"\n\n\"Mars Tom, does you reckon dey's any o' dat kind o' salve in de worl'\nnow?\"\n\n\"Yes, Uncle Abner says there is. He says they've got it in New York, and\nthey put it on country people's eyes and show them all the railroads in\nthe world, and they go in and git them, and then when they rub the salve\non the other eye the other man bids them goodbye and goes off with their\nrailroads. Here's the treasure-hill now. Lower away!\"\n\nWe landed, but it warn't as interesting as I thought it was going to\nbe, because we couldn't find the place where they went in to git the\ntreasure. Still, it was plenty interesting enough, just to see the mere\nhill itself where such a wonderful thing happened. Jim said he wou'dn't\n'a' missed it for three dollars, and I felt the same way.\n\nAnd to me and Jim, as wonderful a thing as any was the way Tom could\ncome into a strange big country like this and go straight and find a\nlittle hump like that and tell it in a minute from a million other humps\nthat was almost just like it, and nothing to help him but only his own\nlearning and his own natural smartness. We talked and talked it over\ntogether, but couldn't make out how he done it. He had the best head on\nhim I ever see; and all he lacked was age, to make a name for himself\nequal to Captain Kidd or George Washington. I bet you it would 'a'\ncrowded either of THEM to find that hill, with all their gifts, but it\nwarn't nothing to Tom Sawyer; he went across Sahara and put his finger\non it as easy as you could pick a nigger out of a bunch of angels.\n\nWe found a pond of salt water close by and scraped up a raft of salt\naround the edges, and loaded up the lion's skin and the tiger's so as\nthey would keep till Jim could tan them.\n\n\n\nCHAPTER XI. THE SAND-STORM\n\nWE went a-fooling along for a day or two, and then just as the full moon\nwas touching the ground on the other side of the desert, we see a string\nof little black figgers moving across its big silver face. You could\nsee them as plain as if they was painted on the moon with ink. It was\nanother caravan. We cooled down our speed and tagged along after it,\njust to have company, though it warn't going our way. It was a rattler,\nthat caravan, and a most bully sight to look at next morning when the\nsun come a-streaming across the desert and flung the long shadders of\nthe camels on the gold sand like a thousand grand-daddy-long-legses\nmarching in procession. We never went very near it, because we knowed\nbetter now than to act like that and scare people's camels and break up\ntheir caravans. It was the gayest outfit you ever see, for rich clothes\nand nobby style. Some of the chiefs rode on dromedaries, the first we\never see, and very tall, and they go plunging along like they was on\nstilts, and they rock the man that is on them pretty violent and churn\nup his dinner considerable, I bet you, but they make noble good time,\nand a camel ain't nowheres with them for speed.\n\nThe caravan camped, during the middle part of the day, and then started\nagain about the middle of the afternoon. Before long the sun begun to\nlook very curious. First it kind of turned to brass, and then to copper,\nand after that it begun to look like a blood-red ball, and the air got\nhot and close, and pretty soon all the sky in the west darkened up and\nlooked thick and foggy, but fiery and dreadful--like it looks through\na piece of red glass, you know. We looked down and see a big confusion\ngoing on in the caravan, and a rushing every which way like they was\nscared; and then they all flopped down flat in the sand and laid there\nperfectly still.\n\nPretty soon we see something coming that stood up like an amazing wide\nwall, and reached from the Desert up into the sky and hid the sun, and\nit was coming like the nation, too. Then a little faint breeze struck\nus, and then it come harder, and grains of sand begun to sift against\nour faces and sting like fire, and Tom sung out:\n\n\"It's a sand-storm--turn your backs to it!\"\n\nWe done it; and in another minute it was blowing a gale, and the sand\nbeat against us by the shovelful, and the air was so thick with it we\ncouldn't see a thing. In five minutes the boat was level full, and we\nwas setting on the lockers buried up to the chin in sand, and only our\nheads out and could hardly breathe.\n\nThen the storm thinned, and we see that monstrous wall go a-sailing off\nacross the desert, awful to look at, I tell you. We dug ourselves out\nand looked down, and where the caravan was before there wasn't anything\nbut just the sand ocean now, and all still and quiet. All them people\nand camels was smothered and dead and buried--buried under ten foot of\nsand, we reckoned, and Tom allowed it might be years before the wind\nuncovered them, and all that time their friends wouldn't ever know what\nbecome of that caravan. Tom said:\n\n\"NOW we know what it was that happened to the people we got the swords\nand pistols from.\"\n\nYes, sir, that was just it. It was as plain as day now. They got buried\nin a sand-storm, and the wild animals couldn't get at them, and the wind\nnever uncovered them again until they was dried to leather and warn't\nfit to eat. It seemed to me we had felt as sorry for them poor people as\na person could for anybody, and as mournful, too, but we was mistaken;\nthis last caravan's death went harder with us, a good deal harder.\nYou see, the others was total strangers, and we never got to feeling\nacquainted with them at all, except, maybe, a little with the man that\nwas watching the girl, but it was different with this last caravan. We\nwas huvvering around them a whole night and 'most a whole day, and had\ngot to feeling real friendly with them, and acquainted. I have found\nout that there ain't no surer way to find out whether you like people or\nhate them than to travel with them. Just so with these. We kind of liked\nthem from the start, and traveling with them put on the finisher. The\nlonger we traveled with them, and the more we got used to their ways,\nthe better and better we liked them, and the gladder and gladder we was\nthat we run across them. We had come to know some of them so well that\nwe called them by name when we was talking about them, and soon got so\nfamiliar and sociable that we even dropped the Miss and Mister and just\nused their plain names without any handle, and it did not seem unpolite,\nbut just the right thing. Of course, it wasn't their own names, but\nnames we give them. There was Mr. Elexander Robinson and Miss Adaline\nRobinson, and Colonel Jacob McDougal and Miss Harryet McDougal, and\nJudge Jeremiah Butler and young Bushrod Butler, and these was big chiefs\nmostly that wore splendid great turbans and simmeters, and dressed like\nthe Grand Mogul, and their families. But as soon as we come to know them\ngood, and like them very much, it warn't Mister, nor Judge, nor nothing,\nany more, but only Elleck, and Addy, and Jake, and Hattie, and Jerry,\nand Buck, and so on.\n\nAnd you know the more you join in with people in their joys and their\nsorrows, the more nearer and dearer they come to be to you. Now we\nwarn't cold and indifferent, the way most travelers is, we was right\ndown friendly and sociable, and took a chance in everything that was\ngoing, and the caravan could depend on us to be on hand every time, it\ndidn't make no difference what it was.\n\nWhen they camped, we camped right over them, ten or twelve hundred feet\nup in the air. When they et a meal, we et ourn, and it made it ever\nso much home-liker to have their company. When they had a wedding that\nnight, and Buck and Addy got married, we got ourselves up in the very\nstarchiest of the professor's duds for the blow-out, and when they\ndanced we jined in and shook a foot up there.\n\nBut it is sorrow and trouble that brings you the nearest, and it was\na funeral that done it with us. It was next morning, just in the still\ndawn. We didn't know the diseased, and he warn't in our set, but that\nnever made no difference; he belonged to the caravan, and that was\nenough, and there warn't no more sincerer tears shed over him than the\nones we dripped on him from up there eleven hundred foot on high.\n\nYes, parting with this caravan was much more bitterer than it was to\npart with them others, which was comparative strangers, and been dead so\nlong, anyway. We had knowed these in their lives, and was fond of them,\ntoo, and now to have death snatch them from right before our faces while\nwe was looking, and leave us so lonesome and friendless in the middle of\nthat big desert, it did hurt so, and we wished we mightn't ever make\nany more friends on that voyage if we was going to lose them again like\nthat.\n\nWe couldn't keep from talking about them, and they was all the time\ncoming up in our memory, and looking just the way they looked when we\nwas all alive and happy together. We could see the line marching, and\nthe shiny spearheads a-winking in the sun; we could see the dromedaries\nlumbering along; we could see the wedding and the funeral; and more\noftener than anything else we could see them praying, because they don't\nallow nothing to prevent that; whenever the call come, several times a\nday, they would stop right there, and stand up and face to the east, and\nlift back their heads, and spread out their arms and begin, and four or\nfive times they would go down on their knees, and then fall forward and\ntouch their forehead to the ground.\n\nWell, it warn't good to go on talking about them, lovely as they was\nin their life, and dear to us in their life and death both, because\nit didn't do no good, and made us too down-hearted. Jim allowed he was\ngoing to live as good a life as he could, so he could see them again\nin a better world; and Tom kept still and didn't tell him they was only\nMohammedans; it warn't no use to disappoint him, he was feeling bad\nenough just as it was.\n\nWhen we woke up next morning we was feeling a little cheerfuller, and\nhad had a most powerful good sleep, because sand is the comfortablest\nbed there is, and I don't see why people that can afford it don't have\nit more. And it's terrible good ballast, too; I never see the balloon so\nsteady before.\n\nTom allowed we had twenty tons of it, and wondered what we better do\nwith it; it was good sand, and it didn't seem good sense to throw it\naway. Jim says:\n\n\"Mars Tom, can't we tote it back home en sell it? How long'll it take?\"\n\n\"Depends on the way we go.\"\n\n\"Well, sah, she's wuth a quarter of a dollar a load at home, en I reckon\nwe's got as much as twenty loads, hain't we? How much would dat be?\"\n\n\"Five dollars.\"\n\n\"By jings, Mars Tom, le's shove for home right on de spot! Hit's more'n\na dollar en a half apiece, hain't it?\"\n\n\"Yes.\"\n\n\"Well, ef dat ain't makin' money de easiest ever I struck! She jes'\nrained in--never cos' us a lick o' work. Le's mosey right along, Mars\nTom.\"\n\nBut Tom was thinking and ciphering away so busy and excited he never\nheard him. Pretty soon he says:\n\n\"Five dollars--sho! Look here, this sand's worth--worth--why, it's worth\nno end of money.\"\n\n\"How is dat, Mars Tom? Go on, honey, go on!\"\n\n\"Well, the minute people knows it's genuwyne sand from the genuwyne\nDesert of Sahara, they'll just be in a perfect state of mind to git hold\nof some of it to keep on the what-not in a vial with a label on it for\na curiosity. All we got to do is to put it up in vials and float around\nall over the United States and peddle them out at ten cents apiece.\nWe've got all of ten thousand dollars' worth of sand in this boat.\"\n\nMe and Jim went all to pieces with joy, and begun to shout\nwhoopjamboreehoo, and Tom says:\n\n\"And we can keep on coming back and fetching sand, and coming back and\nfetching more sand, and just keep it a-going till we've carted this\nwhole Desert over there and sold it out; and there ain't ever going to\nbe any opposition, either, because we'll take out a patent.\"\n\n\"My goodness,\" I says, \"we'll be as rich as Creosote, won't we, Tom?\"\n\n\"Yes--Creesus, you mean. Why, that dervish was hunting in that little\nhill for the treasures of the earth, and didn't know he was walking\nover the real ones for a thousand miles. He was blinder than he made the\ndriver.\"\n\n\"Mars Tom, how much is we gwyne to be worth?\"\n\n\"Well, I don't know yet. It's got to be ciphered, and it ain't the\neasiest job to do, either, because it's over four million square miles\nof sand at ten cents a vial.\"\n\nJim was awful excited, but this faded it out considerable, and he shook\nhis head and says:\n\n\"Mars Tom, we can't 'ford all dem vials--a king couldn't. We better not\ntry to take de whole Desert, Mars Tom, de vials gwyne to bust us, sho'.\"\n\nTom's excitement died out, too, now, and I reckoned it was on account\nof the vials, but it wasn't. He set there thinking, and got bluer and\nbluer, and at last he says:\n\n\"Boys, it won't work; we got to give it up.\"\n\n\"Why, Tom?\"\n\n\"On account of the duties.\"\n\nI couldn't make nothing out of that, neither could Jim. I says:\n\n\"What IS our duty, Tom? Because if we can't git around it, why can't we\njust DO it? People often has to.\"\n\nBut he says:\n\n\"Oh, it ain't that kind of duty. The kind I mean is a tax. Whenever you\nstrike a frontier--that's the border of a country, you know--you find a\ncustom-house there, and the gov'ment officers comes and rummages among\nyour things and charges a big tax, which they call a duty because\nit's their duty to bust you if they can, and if you don't pay the duty\nthey'll hog your sand. They call it confiscating, but that don't deceive\nnobody, it's just hogging, and that's all it is. Now if we try to carry\nthis sand home the way we're pointed now, we got to climb fences till we\ngit tired--just frontier after frontier--Egypt, Arabia, Hindostan, and\nso on, and they'll all whack on a duty, and so you see, easy enough, we\nCAN'T go THAT road.\"\n\n\"Why, Tom,\" I says, \"we can sail right over their old frontiers; how are\nTHEY going to stop us?\"\n\nHe looked sorrowful at me, and says, very grave:\n\n\"Huck Finn, do you think that would be honest?\"\n\nI hate them kind of interruptions. I never said nothing, and he went on:\n\n\"Well, we're shut off the other way, too. If we go back the way we've\ncome, there's the New York custom-house, and that is worse than all of\nthem others put together, on account of the kind of cargo we've got.\"\n\n\"Why?\"\n\n\"Well, they can't raise Sahara sand in America, of course, and when they\ncan't raise a thing there, the duty is fourteen hundred thousand per\ncent. on it if you try to fetch it in from where they do raise it.\"\n\n\"There ain't no sense in that, Tom Sawyer.\"\n\n\"Who said there WAS? What do you talk to me like that for, Huck Finn?\nYou wait till I say a thing's got sense in it before you go to accusing\nme of saying it.\"\n\n\"All right, consider me crying about it, and sorry. Go on.\"\n\nJim says:\n\n\"Mars Tom, do dey jam dat duty onto everything we can't raise in\nAmerica, en don't make no 'stinction 'twix' anything?\"\n\n\"Yes, that's what they do.\"\n\n\"Mars Tom, ain't de blessin' o' de Lord de mos' valuable thing dey is?\"\n\n\"Yes, it is.\"\n\n\"Don't de preacher stan' up in de pulpit en call it down on de people?\"\n\n\"Yes.\"\n\n\"Whah do it come from?\"\n\n\"From heaven.\"\n\n\"Yassir! you's jes' right, 'deed you is, honey--it come from heaven, en\ndat's a foreign country. NOW, den! do dey put a tax on dat blessin'?\"\n\n\"No, they don't.\"\n\n\"Course dey don't; en so it stan' to reason dat you's mistaken, Mars\nTom. Dey wouldn't put de tax on po' truck like san', dat everybody ain't\n'bleeged to have, en leave it off'n de bes' thing dey is, which nobody\ncan't git along widout.\"\n\nTom Sawyer was stumped; he see Jim had got him where he couldn't budge.\nHe tried to wiggle out by saying they had FORGOT to put on that tax, but\nthey'd be sure to remember about it, next session of Congress, and then\nthey'd put it on, but that was a poor lame come-off, and he knowed it.\nHe said there warn't nothing foreign that warn't taxed but just that\none, and so they couldn't be consistent without taxing it, and to be\nconsistent was the first law of politics. So he stuck to it that they'd\nleft it out unintentional and would be certain to do their best to fix\nit before they got caught and laughed at.\n\nBut I didn't feel no more interest in such things, as long as we\ncouldn't git our sand through, and it made me low-spirited, and Jim the\nsame. Tom he tried to cheer us up by saying he would think up another\nspeculation for us that would be just as good as this one and better,\nbut it didn't do no good, we didn't believe there was any as big as\nthis. It was mighty hard; such a little while ago we was so rich, and\ncould 'a' bought a country and started a kingdom and been celebrated and\nhappy, and now we was so poor and ornery again, and had our sand left\non our hands. The sand was looking so lovely before, just like gold and\ndi'monds, and the feel of it was so soft and so silky and nice, but now\nI couldn't bear the sight of it, it made me sick to look at it, and I\nknowed I wouldn't ever feel comfortable again till we got shut of it,\nand I didn't have it there no more to remind us of what we had been and\nwhat we had got degraded down to. The others was feeling the same way\nabout it that I was. I knowed it, because they cheered up so, the minute\nI says le's throw this truck overboard.\n\nWell, it was going to be work, you know, and pretty solid work, too; so\nTom he divided it up according to fairness and strength. He said me and\nhim would clear out a fifth apiece of the sand, and Jim three-fifths.\nJim he didn't quite like that arrangement. He says:\n\n\"Course I's de stronges', en I's willin' to do a share accordin', but by\njings you's kinder pilin' it onto ole Jim, Mars Tom, hain't you?\"\n\n\"Well, I didn't think so, Jim, but you try your hand at fixing it, and\nlet's see.\"\n\nSo Jim reckoned it wouldn't be no more than fair if me and Tom done a\nTENTH apiece. Tom he turned his back to git room and be private, and\nthen he smole a smile that spread around and covered the whole Sahara to\nthe westward, back to the Atlantic edge of it where we come from. Then\nhe turned around again and said it was a good enough arrangement, and we\nwas satisfied if Jim was. Jim said he was.\n\nSo then Tom measured off our two-tenths in the bow and left the rest for\nJim, and it surprised Jim a good deal to see how much difference there\nwas and what a raging lot of sand his share come to, and said he\nwas powerful glad now that he had spoke up in time and got the first\narrangement altered, for he said that even the way it was now, there was\nmore sand than enjoyment in his end of the contract, he believed.\n\nThen we laid into it. It was mighty hot work, and tough; so hot we had\nto move up into cooler weather or we couldn't 'a' stood it. Me and Tom\ntook turn about, and one worked while t'other rested, but there warn't\nnobody to spell poor old Jim, and he made all that part of Africa damp,\nhe sweated so. We couldn't work good, we was so full of laugh, and Jim\nhe kept fretting and wanting to know what tickled us so, and we had\nto keep making up things to account for it, and they was pretty poor\ninventions, but they done well enough, Jim didn't see through them.\nAt last when we got done we was 'most dead, but not with work but with\nlaughing. By and by Jim was 'most dead, too, but: it was with work; then\nwe took turns and spelled him, and he was as thankfull as he could be,\nand would set on the gunnel and swab the sweat, and heave and pant, and\nsay how good we was to a poor old nigger, and he wouldn't ever forgit\nus. He was always the gratefulest nigger I ever see, for any little\nthing you done for him. He was only nigger outside; inside he was as\nwhite as you be.\n\n\n\nCHAPTER XII. JIM STANDING SIEGE\n\nTHE next few meals was pretty sandy, but that don't make no difference\nwhen you are hungry; and when you ain't it ain't no satisfaction to eat,\nanyway, and so a little grit in the meat ain't no particular drawback,\nas far as I can see.\n\nThen we struck the east end of the Desert at last, sailing on a\nnortheast course. Away off on the edge of the sand, in a soft pinky\nlight, we see three little sharp roofs like tents, and Tom says:\n\n\"It's the pyramids of Egypt.\"\n\nIt made my heart fairly jump. You see, I had seen a many and a many a\npicture of them, and heard tell about them a hundred times, and yet to\ncome on them all of a sudden, that way, and find they was REAL, 'stead\nof imaginations, 'most knocked the breath out of me with surprise. It's\na curious thing, that the more you hear about a grand and big and bully\nthing or person, the more it kind of dreamies out, as you may say, and\ngets to be a big dim wavery figger made out of moonshine and nothing\nsolid to it. It's just so with George Washington, and the same with them\npyramids.\n\nAnd moreover, besides, the thing they always said about them seemed to\nme to be stretchers. There was a feller come to the Sunday-school once,\nand had a picture of them, and made a speech, and said the biggest\npyramid covered thirteen acres, and was most five hundred foot high,\njust a steep mountain, all built out of hunks of stone as big as a\nbureau, and laid up in perfectly regular layers, like stair-steps.\nThirteen acres, you see, for just one building; it's a farm. If it\nhadn't been in Sunday-school, I would 'a' judged it was a lie; and\noutside I was certain of it. And he said there was a hole in the\npyramid, and you could go in there with candles, and go ever so far up\na long slanting tunnel, and come to a large room in the stomach of that\nstone mountain, and there you would find a big stone chest with a king\nin it, four thousand years old. I said to myself, then, if that ain't\na lie I will eat that king if they will fetch him, for even Methusalem\nwarn't that old, and nobody claims it.\n\nAs we come a little nearer we see the yaller sand come to an end in\na long straight edge like a blanket, and on to it was joined, edge\nto edge, a wide country of bright green, with a snaky stripe crooking\nthrough it, and Tom said it was the Nile. It made my heart jump again,\nfor the Nile was another thing that wasn't real to me. Now I can tell\nyou one thing which is dead certain: if you will fool along over three\nthousand miles of yaller sand, all glimmering with heat so that it makes\nyour eyes water to look at it, and you've been a considerable part of\na week doing it, the green country will look so like home and heaven to\nyou that it will make your eyes water AGAIN.\n\nIt was just so with me, and the same with Jim.\n\nAnd when Jim got so he could believe it WAS the land of Egypt he was\nlooking at, he wouldn't enter it standing up, but got down on his knees\nand took off his hat, because he said it wasn't fitten' for a humble\npoor nigger to come any other way where such men had been as Moses and\nJoseph and Pharaoh and the other prophets. He was a Presbyterian, and\nhad a most deep respect for Moses which was a Presbyterian, too, he\nsaid. He was all stirred up, and says:\n\n\"Hit's de lan' of Egypt, de lan' of Egypt, en I's 'lowed to look at\nit wid my own eyes! En dah's de river dat was turn' to blood, en I's\nlooking at de very same groun' whah de plagues was, en de lice, en de\nfrogs, en de locus', en de hail, en whah dey marked de door-pos', en de\nangel o' de Lord come by in de darkness o' de night en slew de fust-born\nin all de lan' o' Egypt. Ole Jim ain't worthy to see dis day!\"\n\nAnd then he just broke down and cried, he was so thankful. So between\nhim and Tom there was talk enough, Jim being excited because the\nland was so full of history--Joseph and his brethren, Moses in the\nbulrushers, Jacob coming down into Egypt to buy corn, the silver cup in\nthe sack, and all them interesting things; and Tom just as excited too,\nbecause the land was so full of history that was in HIS line, about\nNoureddin, and Bedreddin, and such like monstrous giants, that made\nJim's wool rise, and a raft of other Arabian Nights folks, which the\nhalf of them never done the things they let on they done, I don't\nbelieve.\n\nThen we struck a disappointment, for one of them early morning fogs\nstarted up, and it warn't no use to sail over the top of it, because we\nwould go by Egypt, sure, so we judged it was best to set her by compass\nstraight for the place where the pyramids was gitting blurred and\nblotted out, and then drop low and skin along pretty close to the ground\nand keep a sharp lookout. Tom took the hellum, I stood by to let go the\nanchor, and Jim he straddled the bow to dig through the fog with his\neyes and watch out for danger ahead. We went along a steady gait, but\nnot very fast, and the fog got solider and solider, so solid that Jim\nlooked dim and ragged and smoky through it. It was awful still, and we\ntalked low and was anxious. Now and then Jim would say:\n\n\"Highst her a p'int, Mars Tom, highst her!\" and up she would skip, a\nfoot or two, and we would slide right over a flat-roofed mud cabin, with\npeople that had been asleep on it just beginning to turn out and gap\nand stretch; and once when a feller was clear up on his hind legs so he\ncould gap and stretch better, we took him a blip in the back and knocked\nhim off. By and by, after about an hour, and everything dead still\nand we a-straining our ears for sounds and holding our breath, the fog\nthinned a little, very sudden, and Jim sung out in an awful scare:\n\n\"Oh, for de lan's sake, set her back, Mars Tom, here's de biggest giant\nouten de 'Rabian Nights a-comin' for us!\" and he went over backwards in\nthe boat.\n\nTom slammed on the back-action, and as we slowed to a standstill a man's\nface as big as our house at home looked in over the gunnel, same as a\nhouse looks out of its windows, and I laid down and died. I must 'a'\nbeen clear dead and gone for as much as a minute or more; then I come\nto, and Tom had hitched a boat-hook on to the lower lip of the giant and\nwas holding the balloon steady with it whilst he canted his head back\nand got a good long look up at that awful face.\n\nJim was on his knees with his hands clasped, gazing up at the thing in a\nbegging way, and working his lips, but not getting anything out. I took\nonly just a glimpse, and was fading out again, but Tom says:\n\n\"He ain't alive, you fools; it's the Sphinx!\"\n\nI never see Tom look so little and like a fly; but that was because\nthe giant's head was so big and awful. Awful, yes, so it was, but not\ndreadful any more, because you could see it was a noble face, and kind\nof sad, and not thinking about you, but about other things and larger.\nIt was stone, reddish stone, and its nose and ears battered, and that\ngive it an abused look, and you felt sorrier for it for that.\n\nWe stood off a piece, and sailed around it and over it, and it was just\ngrand. It was a man's head, or maybe a woman's, on a tiger's body a\nhundred and twenty-five foot long, and there was a dear little temple\nbetween its front paws. All but the head used to be under the sand, for\nhundreds of years, maybe thousands, but they had just lately dug the\nsand away and found that little temple. It took a power of sand to bury\nthat cretur; most as much as it would to bury a steamboat, I reckon.\n\nWe landed Jim on top of the head, with an American flag to protect him,\nit being a foreign land; then we sailed off to this and that and\nt'other distance, to git what Tom called effects and perspectives\nand proportions, and Jim he done the best he could, striking all the\ndifferent kinds of attitudes and positions he could study up, but\nstanding on his head and working his legs the way a frog does was the\nbest. The further we got away, the littler Jim got, and the grander\nthe Sphinx got, till at last it was only a clothespin on a dome, as\nyou might say. That's the way perspective brings out the correct\nproportions, Tom said; he said Julus Cesar's niggers didn't know how big\nhe was, they was too close to him.\n\nThen we sailed off further and further, till we couldn't see Jim at all\nany more, and then that great figger was at its noblest, a-gazing out\nover the Nile Valley so still and solemn and lonesome, and all the\nlittle shabby huts and things that was scattered about it clean\ndisappeared and gone, and nothing around it now but a soft wide spread\nof yaller velvet, which was the sand.\n\nThat was the right place to stop, and we done it. We set there a-looking\nand a-thinking for a half an hour, nobody a-saying anything, for it made\nus feel quiet and kind of solemn to remember it had been looking over\nthat valley just that same way, and thinking its awful thoughts all to\nitself for thousands of years, and nobody can't find out what they are\nto this day.\n\nAt last I took up the glass and see some little black things a-capering\naround on that velvet carpet, and some more a-climbing up the cretur's\nback, and then I see two or three wee puffs of white smoke, and told Tom\nto look. He done it, and says:\n\n\"They're bugs. No--hold on; they--why, I believe they're men. Yes, it's\nmen--men and horses both. They're hauling a long ladder up onto the\nSphinx's back--now ain't that odd? And now they're trying to lean it\nup a--there's some more puffs of smoke--it's guns! Huck, they're after\nJim.\"\n\nWe clapped on the power, and went for them a-biling. We was there in\nno time, and come a-whizzing down amongst them, and they broke and\nscattered every which way, and some that was climbing the ladder after\nJim let go all holts and fell. We soared up and found him laying on top\nof the head panting and most tuckered out, partly from howling for help\nand partly from scare. He had been standing a siege a long time--a week,\nHE said, but it warn't so, it only just seemed so to him because they\nwas crowding him so. They had shot at him, and rained the bullets all\naround him, but he warn't hit, and when they found he wouldn't stand up\nand the bullets couldn't git at him when he was laying down, they went\nfor the ladder, and then he knowed it was all up with him if we didn't\ncome pretty quick. Tom was very indignant, and asked him why he didn't\nshow the flag and command them to GIT, in the name of the United States.\nJim said he done it, but they never paid no attention. Tom said he would\nhave this thing looked into at Washington, and says:\n\n\"You'll see that they'll have to apologize for insulting the flag, and\npay an indemnity, too, on top of it even if they git off THAT easy.\"\n\nJim says:\n\n\"What's an indemnity, Mars Tom?\"\n\n\"It's cash, that's what it is.\"\n\n\"Who gits it, Mars Tom?\"\n\n\"Why, WE do.\"\n\n\"En who gits de apology?\"\n\n\"The United States. Or, we can take whichever we please. We can take the\napology, if we want to, and let the gov'ment take the money.\"\n\n\"How much money will it be, Mars Tom?\"\n\n\"Well, in an aggravated case like this one, it will be at least three\ndollars apiece, and I don't know but more.\"\n\n\"Well, den, we'll take de money, Mars Tom, blame de 'pology. Hain't dat\nyo' notion, too? En hain't it yourn, Huck?\"\n\nWe talked it over a little and allowed that that was as good a way as\nany, so we agreed to take the money. It was a new business to me, and I\nasked Tom if countries always apologized when they had done wrong, and\nhe says:\n\n\"Yes; the little ones does.\"\n\nWe was sailing around examining the pyramids, you know, and now we\nsoared up and roosted on the flat top of the biggest one, and found it\nwas just like what the man said in the Sunday-school. It was like four\npairs of stairs that starts broad at the bottom and slants up and comes\ntogether in a point at the top, only these stair-steps couldn't be clumb\nthe way you climb other stairs; no, for each step was as high as your\nchin, and you have to be boosted up from behind. The two other pyramids\nwarn't far away, and the people moving about on the sand between looked\nlike bugs crawling, we was so high above them.\n\nTom he couldn't hold himself he was so worked up with gladness and\nastonishment to be in such a celebrated place, and he just dripped\nhistory from every pore, seemed to me. He said he couldn't scarcely\nbelieve he was standing on the very identical spot the prince flew\nfrom on the Bronze Horse. It was in the Arabian Night times, he said.\nSomebody give the prince a bronze horse with a peg in its shoulder, and\nhe could git on him and fly through the air like a bird, and go all over\nthe world, and steer it by turning the peg, and fly high or low and land\nwherever he wanted to.\n\nWhen he got done telling it there was one of them uncomfortable silences\nthat comes, you know, when a person has been telling a whopper and you\nfeel sorry for him and wish you could think of some way to change the\nsubject and let him down easy, but git stuck and don't see no way, and\nbefore you can pull your mind together and DO something, that silence\nhas got in and spread itself and done the business. I was embarrassed,\nJim he was embarrassed, and neither of us couldn't say a word. Well, Tom\nhe glowered at me a minute, and says:\n\n\"Come, out with it. What do you think?\"\n\nI says:\n\n\"Tom Sawyer, YOU don't believe that, yourself.\"\n\n\"What's the reason I don't? What's to hender me?\"\n\n\"There's one thing to hender you: it couldn't happen, that's all.\"\n\n\"What's the reason it couldn't happen?\"\n\n\"You tell me the reason it COULD happen.\"\n\n\"This balloon is a good enough reason it could happen, I should reckon.\"\n\n\"WHY is it?\"\n\n\"WHY is it? I never saw such an idiot. Ain't this balloon and the bronze\nhorse the same thing under different names?\"\n\n\"No, they're not. One is a balloon and the other's a horse. It's very\ndifferent. Next you'll be saying a house and a cow is the same thing.\"\n\n\"By Jackson, Huck's got him ag'in! Dey ain't no wigglin' outer dat!\"\n\n\"Shut your head, Jim; you don't know what you're talking about. And\nHuck don't. Look here, Huck, I'll make it plain to you, so you can\nunderstand. You see, it ain't the mere FORM that's got anything to do\nwith their being similar or unsimilar, it's the PRINCIPLE involved; and\nthe principle is the same in both. Don't you see, now?\"\n\nI turned it over in my mind, and says:\n\n\"Tom, it ain't no use. Principles is all very well, but they don't git\naround that one big fact, that the thing that a balloon can do ain't no\nsort of proof of what a horse can do.\"\n\n\"Shucks, Huck, you don't get the idea at all. Now look here a\nminute--it's perfectly plain. Don't we fly through the air?\"\n\n\"Yes.\"\n\n\"Very well. Don't we fly high or fly low, just as we please?\"\n\n\"Yes.\"\n\n\"Don't we steer whichever way we want to?\"\n\n\"Yes.\"\n\n\"And don't we land when and where we please?\"\n\n\"Yes.\"\n\n\"How do we move the balloon and steer it?\"\n\n\"By touching the buttons.\"\n\n\"NOW I reckon the thing is clear to you at last. In the other case the\nmoving and steering was done by turning a peg. We touch a button, the\nprince turned a peg. There ain't an atom of difference, you see. I\nknowed I could git it through your head if I stuck to it long enough.\"\n\nHe felt so happy he begun to whistle. But me and Jim was silent, so he\nbroke off surprised, and says:\n\n\"Looky here, Huck Finn, don't you see it YET?\"\n\nI says:\n\n\"Tom Sawyer, I want to ask you some questions.\"\n\n\"Go ahead,\" he says, and I see Jim chirk up to listen.\n\n\"As I understand it, the whole thing is in the buttons and the peg--the\nrest ain't of no consequence. A button is one shape, a peg is another\nshape, but that ain't any matter?\"\n\n\"No, that ain't any matter, as long as they've both got the same power.\"\n\n\"All right, then. What is the power that's in a candle and in a match?\"\n\n\"It's the fire.\"\n\n\"It's the same in both, then?\"\n\n\"Yes, just the same in both.\"\n\n\"All right. Suppose I set fire to a carpenter shop with a match, what\nwill happen to that carpenter shop?\"\n\n\"She'll burn up.\"\n\n\"And suppose I set fire to this pyramid with a candle--will she burn\nup?\"\n\n\"Of course she won't.\"\n\n\"All right. Now the fire's the same, both times. WHY does the shop burn,\nand the pyramid don't?\"\n\n\"Because the pyramid CAN'T burn.\"\n\n\"Aha! and A HORSE CAN'T FLY!\"\n\n\"My lan', ef Huck ain't got him ag'in! Huck's landed him high en dry\ndis time, I tell you! Hit's de smartes' trap I ever see a body walk\ninter--en ef I--\"\n\nBut Jim was so full of laugh he got to strangling and couldn't go on,\nand Tom was that mad to see how neat I had floored him, and turned his\nown argument ag'in him and knocked him all to rags and flinders with it,\nthat all he could manage to say was that whenever he heard me and\nJim try to argue it made him ashamed of the human race. I never said\nnothing; I was feeling pretty well satisfied. When I have got the best\nof a person that way, it ain't my way to go around crowing about it\nthe way some people does, for I consider that if I was in his place I\nwouldn't wish him to crow over me. It's better to be generous, that's\nwhat I think.\n\n\n\nCHAPTER XIII. GOING FOR TOM'S PIPE:\n\nBY AND BY we left Jim to float around up there in the neighborhood\nof the pyramids, and we clumb down to the hole where you go into the\ntunnel, and went in with some Arabs and candles, and away in there in\nthe middle of the pyramid we found a room and a big stone box in it\nwhere they used to keep that king, just as the man in the Sunday-school\nsaid; but he was gone, now; somebody had got him. But I didn't take no\ninterest in the place, because there could be ghosts there, of course;\nnot fresh ones, but I don't like no kind.\n\nSo then we come out and got some little donkeys and rode a piece, and\nthen went in a boat another piece, and then more donkeys, and got to\nCairo; and all the way the road was as smooth and beautiful a road as\never I see, and had tall date-pa'ms on both sides, and naked children\neverywhere, and the men was as red as copper, and fine and strong and\nhandsome. And the city was a curiosity. Such narrow streets--why, they\nwere just lanes, and crowded with people with turbans, and women with\nveils, and everybody rigged out in blazing bright clothes and all sorts\nof colors, and you wondered how the camels and the people got by each\nother in such narrow little cracks, but they done it--a perfect jam, you\nsee, and everybody noisy. The stores warn't big enough to turn around\nin, but you didn't have to go in; the storekeeper sat tailor fashion on\nhis counter, smoking his snaky long pipe, and had his things where he\ncould reach them to sell, and he was just as good as in the street, for\nthe camel-loads brushed him as they went by.\n\nNow and then a grand person flew by in a carriage with fancy dressed men\nrunning and yelling in front of it and whacking anybody with a long rod\nthat didn't get out of the way. And by and by along comes the Sultan\nriding horseback at the head of a procession, and fairly took your\nbreath away his clothes was so splendid; and everybody fell flat and\nlaid on his stomach while he went by. I forgot, but a feller helped me\nto remember. He was one that had a rod and run in front.\n\nThere was churches, but they don't know enough to keep Sunday; they keep\nFriday and break the Sabbath. You have to take off your shoes when you\ngo in. There was crowds of men and boys in the church, setting in groups\non the stone floor and making no end of noise--getting their lessons\nby heart, Tom said, out of the Koran, which they think is a Bible, and\npeople that knows better knows enough to not let on. I never see such a\nbig church in my life before, and most awful high, it was; it made you\ndizzy to look up; our village church at home ain't a circumstance to it;\nif you was to put it in there, people would think it was a drygoods box.\n\nWhat I wanted to see was a dervish, because I was interested in\ndervishes on accounts of the one that played the trick on the\ncamel-driver. So we found a lot in a kind of a church, and they called\nthemselves Whirling Dervishes; and they did whirl, too. I never\nsee anything like it. They had tall sugar-loaf hats on, and linen\npetticoats; and they spun and spun and spun, round and round like tops,\nand the petticoats stood out on a slant, and it was the prettiest thing\nI ever see, and made me drunk to look at it. They was all Moslems, Tom\nsaid, and when I asked him what a Moslem was, he said it was a person\nthat wasn't a Presbyterian. So there is plenty of them in Missouri,\nthough I didn't know it before.\n\nWe didn't see half there was to see in Cairo, because Tom was in such a\nsweat to hunt out places that was celebrated in history. We had a most\ntiresome time to find the granary where Joseph stored up the grain\nbefore the famine, and when we found it it warn't worth much to look\nat, being such an old tumble-down wreck; but Tom was satisfied, and made\nmore fuss over it than I would make if I stuck a nail in my foot. How\nhe ever found that place was too many for me. We passed as much as forty\njust like it before we come to it, and any of them would 'a' done for\nme, but none but just the right one would suit him; I never see anybody\nso particular as Tom Sawyer. The minute he struck the right one he\nreconnized it as easy as I would reconnize my other shirt if I had one,\nbut how he done it he couldn't any more tell than he could fly; he said\nso himself.\n\nThen we hunted a long time for the house where the boy lived that\nlearned the cadi how to try the case of the old olives and the new ones,\nand said it was out of the Arabian Nights, and he would tell me and Jim\nabout it when he got time. Well, we hunted and hunted till I was ready\nto drop, and I wanted Tom to give it up and come next day and git\nsomebody that knowed the town and could talk Missourian and could go\nstraight to the place; but no, he wanted to find it himself, and nothing\nelse would answer. So on we went. Then at last the remarkablest\nthing happened I ever see. The house was gone--gone hundreds of years\nago--every last rag of it gone but just one mud brick. Now a person\nwouldn't ever believe that a backwoods Missouri boy that hadn't ever\nbeen in that town before could go and hunt that place over and find that\nbrick, but Tom Sawyer done it. I know he done it, because I see him do\nit. I was right by his very side at the time, and see him see the brick\nand see him reconnize it. Well, I says to myself, how DOES he do it? Is\nit knowledge, or is it instink?\n\nNow there's the facts, just as they happened: let everybody explain it\ntheir own way. I've ciphered over it a good deal, and it's my opinion\nthat some of it is knowledge but the main bulk of it is instink. The\nreason is this: Tom put the brick in his pocket to give to a museum with\nhis name on it and the facts when he went home, and I slipped it out and\nput another brick considerable like it in its place, and he didn't\nknow the difference--but there was a difference, you see. I think that\nsettles it--it's mostly instink, not knowledge. Instink tells him where\nthe exact PLACE is for the brick to be in, and so he reconnizes it by\nthe place it's in, not by the look of the brick. If it was knowledge,\nnot instink, he would know the brick again by the look of it the next\ntime he seen it--which he didn't. So it shows that for all the brag\nyou hear about knowledge being such a wonderful thing, instink is worth\nforty of it for real unerringness. Jim says the same.\n\nWhen we got back Jim dropped down and took us in, and there was a young\nman there with a red skullcap and tassel on and a beautiful silk jacket\nand baggy trousers with a shawl around his waist and pistols in it that\ncould talk English and wanted to hire to us as guide and take us to\nMecca and Medina and Central Africa and everywheres for a half a dollar\na day and his keep, and we hired him and left, and piled on the power,\nand by the time we was through dinner we was over the place where the\nIsraelites crossed the Red Sea when Pharaoh tried to overtake them and\nwas caught by the waters. We stopped, then, and had a good look at the\nplace, and it done Jim good to see it. He said he could see it all,\nnow, just the way it happened; he could see the Israelites walking along\nbetween the walls of water, and the Egyptians coming, from away off\nyonder, hurrying all they could, and see them start in as the Israelites\nwent out, and then when they was all in, see the walls tumble together\nand drown the last man of them. Then we piled on the power again and\nrushed away and huvvered over Mount Sinai, and saw the place where Moses\nbroke the tables of stone, and where the children of Israel camped\nin the plain and worshiped the golden calf, and it was all just as\ninteresting as could be, and the guide knowed every place as well as I\nknowed the village at home.\n\nBut we had an accident, now, and it fetched all the plans to a\nstandstill. Tom's old ornery corn-cob pipe had got so old and swelled\nand warped that she couldn't hold together any longer, notwithstanding\nthe strings and bandages, but caved in and went to pieces. Tom he\ndidn't know WHAT to do. The professor's pipe wouldn't answer; it warn't\nanything but a mershum, and a person that's got used to a cob pipe knows\nit lays a long ways over all the other pipes in this world, and you\ncan't git him to smoke any other. He wouldn't take mine, I couldn't\npersuade him. So there he was.\n\nHe thought it over, and said we must scour around and see if we could\nroust out one in Egypt or Arabia or around in some of these countries,\nbut the guide said no, it warn't no use, they didn't have them. So Tom\nwas pretty glum for a little while, then he chirked up and said he'd got\nthe idea and knowed what to do. He says:\n\n\"I've got another corn-cob pipe, and it's a prime one, too, and nearly\nnew. It's laying on the rafter that's right over the kitchen stove at\nhome in the village. Jim, you and the guide will go and get it, and me\nand Huck will camp here on Mount Sinai till you come back.\"\n\n\"But, Mars Tom, we couldn't ever find de village. I could find de pipe,\n'case I knows de kitchen, but my lan', we can't ever find de village,\nnur Sent Louis, nur none o' dem places. We don't know de way, Mars Tom.\"\n\nThat was a fact, and it stumped Tom for a minute. Then he said:\n\n\"Looky here, it can be done, sure; and I'll tell you how. You set your\ncompass and sail west as straight as a dart, till you find the United\nStates. It ain't any trouble, because it's the first land you'll strike\nthe other side of the Atlantic. If it's daytime when you strike it,\nbulge right on, straight west from the upper part of the Florida\ncoast, and in an hour and three quarters you'll hit the mouth of the\nMississippi--at the speed that I'm going to send you. You'll be so high\nup in the air that the earth will be curved considerable--sorter like\na washbowl turned upside down--and you'll see a raft of rivers crawling\naround every which way, long before you get there, and you can pick out\nthe Mississippi without any trouble. Then you can follow the river north\nnearly, an hour and three quarters, till you see the Ohio come in; then\nyou want to look sharp, because you're getting near. Away up to your\nleft you'll see another thread coming in--that's the Missouri and is a\nlittle above St. Louis. You'll come down low then, so as you can examine\nthe villages as you spin along. You'll pass about twenty-five in the\nnext fifteen minutes, and you'll recognize ours when you see it--and if\nyou don't, you can yell down and ask.\"\n\n\"Ef it's dat easy, Mars Tom, I reckon we kin do it--yassir, I knows we\nkin.\"\n\nThe guide was sure of it, too, and thought that he could learn to stand\nhis watch in a little while.\n\n\"Jim can learn you the whole thing in a half an hour,\" Tom said. \"This\nballoon's as easy to manage as a canoe.\"\n\nTom got out the chart and marked out the course and measured it, and\nsays:\n\n\"To go back west is the shortest way, you see. It's only about seven\nthousand miles. If you went east, and so on around, it's over twice as\nfar.\" Then he says to the guide, \"I want you both to watch the tell-tale\nall through the watches, and whenever it don't mark three hundred miles\nan hour, you go higher or drop lower till you find a storm-current\nthat's going your way. There's a hundred miles an hour in this old thing\nwithout any wind to help. There's two-hundred-mile gales to be found,\nany time you want to hunt for them.\"\n\n\"We'll hunt for them, sir.\"\n\n\"See that you do. Sometimes you may have to go up a couple of miles, and\nit'll be p'ison cold, but most of the time you'll find your storm a good\ndeal lower. If you can only strike a cyclone--that's the ticket for\nyou! You'll see by the professor's books that they travel west in these\nlatitudes; and they travel low, too.\"\n\nThen he ciphered on the time, and says--\n\n\"Seven thousand miles, three hundred miles an hour--you can make the\ntrip in a day--twenty-four hours. This is Thursday; you'll be back here\nSaturday afternoon. Come, now, hustle out some blankets and food and\nbooks and things for me and Huck, and you can start right along. There\nain't no occasion to fool around--I want a smoke, and the quicker you\nfetch that pipe the better.\"\n\nAll hands jumped for the things, and in eight minutes our things was out\nand the balloon was ready for America. So we shook hands good-bye, and\nTom gave his last orders:\n\n\"It's 10 minutes to 2 P.M. now, Mount Sinai time. In 24 hours you'll be\nhome, and it'll be 6 to-morrow morning, village time. When you strike\nthe village, land a little back of the top of the hill, in the woods,\nout of sight; then you rush down, Jim, and shove these letters in the\npost-office, and if you see anybody stirring, pull your slouch down over\nyour face so they won't know you. Then you go and slip in the back way\nto the kitchen and git the pipe, and lay this piece of paper on the\nkitchen table, and put something on it to hold it, and then slide out\nand git away, and don't let Aunt Polly catch a sight of you, nor nobody\nelse. Then you jump for the balloon and shove for Mount Sinai three\nhundred miles an hour. You won't have lost more than an hour. You'll\nstart back at 7 or 8 A.M., village time, and be here in 24 hours,\narriving at 2 or 3 P.M., Mount Sinai time.\"\n\nTom he read the piece of paper to us. He had wrote on it:\n\n     \"THURSDAY AFTERNOON. Tom Sawyer the Erro-nort\n     sends his love to Aunt Polly from Mount Sinai\n     where the Ark was, and so does Huck Finn, and she\n     will get it to-morrow morning half-past six.\" *\n\n  [* This misplacing of the Ark is probably Huck's   error, not\n     Tom's.--M.T.]\n\n\"That'll make her eyes bulge out and the tears come,\" he says. Then he\nsays:\n\n\"Stand by! One--two--three--away you go!\"\n\nAnd away she DID go! Why, she seemed to whiz out of sight in a second.\n\nThen we found a most comfortable cave that looked out over the whole big\nplain, and there we camped to wait for the pipe.\n\nThe balloon come hack all right, and brung the pipe; but Aunt Polly had\ncatched Jim when he was getting it, and anybody can guess what happened:\nshe sent for Tom. So Jim he says:\n\n\"Mars Tom, she's out on de porch wid her eye sot on de sky a-layin' for\nyou, en she say she ain't gwyne to budge from dah tell she gits hold of\nyou. Dey's gwyne to be trouble, Mars Tom, 'deed dey is.\"\n\nSo then we shoved for home, and not feeling very gay, neither.\n\nEND.\n\n\n\n\n\nEnd of Project Gutenberg's Tom Sawyer Abroad, by Mark Twain (Samuel Clemens)\n\n*** END OF THIS PROJECT GUTENBERG EBOOK TOM SAWYER ABROAD ***\n\n***** This file should be named 91.txt or 91.zip *****\nThis and all associated files of various formats will be found in:\n        http://www.gutenberg.org/9/91/\n\nProduced by An Anonymous Volunteer\n\nUpdated editions will replace the previous one--the old editions\nwill be renamed.\n\nCreating the works from public domain print editions means that no\none owns a United States copyright in these works, so the Foundation\n(and you!) can copy and distribute it in the United States without\npermission and without paying copyright royalties. 1805\n\n\n\n\n\nCHAPTER I\n\n\u201cWell, Prince, so Genoa and Lucca are now just family estates of the\nBuonapartes. But I warn you, if you don\u2019t tell me that this means war,\nif you still try to defend the infamies and horrors perpetrated by that\nAntichrist\u2014I really believe he is Antichrist\u2014I will have nothing\nmore to do with you and you are no longer my friend, no longer my\n\u2018faithful slave,\u2019 as you call yourself! But how do you do? I see I\nhave frightened you\u2014sit down and tell me all the news.\u201d\n\nIt was in July, 1805, and the speaker was the well-known Anna P\u00e1vlovna\nSch\u00e9rer, maid of honor and favorite of the Empress M\u00e1rya F\u00ebdorovna.\nWith these words she greeted Prince Vas\u00edli Kur\u00e1gin, a man of high\nrank and importance, who was the first to arrive at her reception. Anna\nP\u00e1vlovna had had a cough for some days. She was, as she said, suffering\nfrom la grippe; grippe being then a new word in St. Petersburg, used\nonly by the elite.\n\nAll her invitations without exception, written in French, and delivered\nby a scarlet-liveried footman that morning, ran as follows:\n\n\u201cIf you have nothing better to do, Count (or Prince), and if the\nprospect of spending an evening with a poor invalid is not too terrible,\nI shall be very charmed to see you tonight between 7 and 10\u2014Annette\nSch\u00e9rer.\u201d\n\n\u201cHeavens! what a virulent attack!\u201d replied the prince, not in the\nleast disconcerted by this reception. He had just entered, wearing an\nembroidered court uniform, knee breeches, and shoes, and had stars on\nhis breast and a serene expression on his flat face. He spoke in that\nrefined French in which our grandfathers not only spoke but thought, and\nwith the gentle, patronizing intonation natural to a man of importance\nwho had grown old in society and at court. He went up to Anna P\u00e1vlovna,\nkissed her hand, presenting to her his bald, scented, and shining head,\nand complacently seated himself on the sofa.\n\n\u201cFirst of all, dear friend, tell me how you are. Set your friend\u2019s\nmind at rest,\u201d said he without altering his tone, beneath the\npoliteness and affected sympathy of which indifference and even irony\ncould be discerned.\n\n\u201cCan one be well while suffering morally? Can one be calm in times\nlike these if one has any feeling?\u201d said Anna P\u00e1vlovna. \u201cYou are\nstaying the whole evening, I hope?\u201d\n\n\u201cAnd the fete at the English ambassador\u2019s? Today is Wednesday. I\nmust put in an appearance there,\u201d said the prince. \u201cMy daughter is\ncoming for me to take me there.\u201d\n\n\u201cI thought today\u2019s fete had been canceled. I confess all these\nfestivities and fireworks are becoming wearisome.\u201d\n\n\u201cIf they had known that you wished it, the entertainment would have\nbeen put off,\u201d said the prince, who, like a wound-up clock, by force\nof habit said things he did not even wish to be believed.\n\n\u201cDon\u2019t tease! Well, and what has been decided about Novos\u00edltsev\u2019s\ndispatch? You know everything.\u201d\n\n\u201cWhat can one say about it?\u201d replied the prince in a cold, listless\ntone. \u201cWhat has been decided? They have decided that Buonaparte has\nburnt his boats, and I believe that we are ready to burn ours.\u201d\n\nPrince Vas\u00edli always spoke languidly, like an actor repeating a stale\npart. Anna P\u00e1vlovna Sch\u00e9rer on the contrary, despite her forty years,\noverflowed with animation and impulsiveness. To be an enthusiast had\nbecome her social vocation and, sometimes even when she did not\nfeel like it, she became enthusiastic in order not to disappoint the\nexpectations of those who knew her. The subdued smile which, though it\ndid not suit her faded features, always played round her lips expressed,\nas in a spoiled child, a continual consciousness of her charming defect,\nwhich she neither wished, nor could, nor considered it necessary, to\ncorrect.\n\nIn the midst of a conversation on political matters Anna P\u00e1vlovna burst\nout:\n\n\u201cOh, don\u2019t speak to me of Austria. Perhaps I don\u2019t understand\nthings, but Austria never has wished, and does not wish, for war. She\nis betraying us! Russia alone must save Europe. Our gracious sovereign\nrecognizes his high vocation and will be true to it. That is the one\nthing I have faith in! Our good and wonderful sovereign has to perform\nthe noblest role on earth, and he is so virtuous and noble that God will\nnot forsake him. He will fulfill his vocation and crush the hydra of\nrevolution, which has become more terrible than ever in the person of\nthis murderer and villain! We alone must avenge the blood of the just\none.... Whom, I ask you, can we rely on?... England with her commercial\nspirit will not and cannot understand the Emperor Alexander\u2019s\nloftiness of soul. She has refused to evacuate Malta. She wanted to\nfind, and still seeks, some secret motive in our actions. What answer\ndid Novos\u00edltsev get? None. The English have not understood and cannot\nunderstand the self-abnegation of our Emperor who wants nothing for\nhimself, but only desires the good of mankind. And what have they\npromised? Nothing! And what little they have promised they will not\nperform! Prussia has always declared that Buonaparte is invincible, and\nthat all Europe is powerless before him.... And I don\u2019t believe a\nword that Hardenburg says, or Haugwitz either. This famous Prussian\nneutrality is just a trap. I have faith only in God and the lofty\ndestiny of our adored monarch. He will save Europe!\u201d\n\nShe suddenly paused, smiling at her own impetuosity.\n\n\u201cI think,\u201d said the prince with a smile, \u201cthat if you had been\nsent instead of our dear Wintzingerode you would have captured the King\nof Prussia\u2019s consent by assault. You are so eloquent. Will you give me\na cup of tea?\u201d\n\n\u201cIn a moment. \u00c0 propos,\u201d she added, becoming calm again, \u201cI am\nexpecting two very interesting men tonight, le Vicomte de Mortemart, who\nis connected with the Montmorencys through the Rohans, one of the best\nFrench families. He is one of the genuine \u00e9migr\u00e9s, the good ones. And\nalso the Abb\u00e9 Morio. Do you know that profound thinker? He has been\nreceived by the Emperor. Had you heard?\u201d\n\n\u201cI shall be delighted to meet them,\u201d said the prince. \u201cBut\ntell me,\u201d he added with studied carelessness as if it had only just\noccurred to him, though the question he was about to ask was the chief\nmotive of his visit, \u201cis it true that the Dowager Empress wants\nBaron Funke to be appointed first secretary at Vienna? The baron by all\naccounts is a poor creature.\u201d\n\nPrince Vas\u00edli wished to obtain this post for his son, but others were\ntrying through the Dowager Empress M\u00e1rya F\u00ebdorovna to secure it for\nthe baron.\n\nAnna P\u00e1vlovna almost closed her eyes to indicate that neither she nor\nanyone else had a right to criticize what the Empress desired or was\npleased with.\n\n\u201cBaron Funke has been recommended to the Dowager Empress by her\nsister,\u201d was all she said, in a dry and mournful tone.\n\nAs she named the Empress, Anna P\u00e1vlovna\u2019s face suddenly assumed an\nexpression of profound and sincere devotion and respect mingled with\nsadness, and this occurred every time she mentioned her illustrious\npatroness. She added that Her Majesty had deigned to show Baron Funke\nbeaucoup d\u2019estime, and again her face clouded over with sadness.\n\nThe prince was silent and looked indifferent. But, with the womanly and\ncourtierlike quickness and tact habitual to her, Anna P\u00e1vlovna\nwished both to rebuke him (for daring to speak as he had done of a man\nrecommended to the Empress) and at the same time to console him, so she\nsaid:\n\n\u201cNow about your family. Do you know that since your daughter came\nout everyone has been enraptured by her? They say she is amazingly\nbeautiful.\u201d\n\nThe prince bowed to signify his respect and gratitude.\n\n\u201cI often think,\u201d she continued after a short pause, drawing nearer\nto the prince and smiling amiably at him as if to show that political\nand social topics were ended and the time had come for intimate\nconversation\u2014\u201cI often think how unfairly sometimes the joys of life\nare distributed. Why has fate given you two such splendid children?\nI don\u2019t speak of Anatole, your youngest. I don\u2019t like him,\u201d she\nadded in a tone admitting of no rejoinder and raising her eyebrows.\n\u201cTwo such charming children. And really you appreciate them less than\nanyone, and so you don\u2019t deserve to have them.\u201d\n\nAnd she smiled her ecstatic smile.\n\n\u201cI can\u2019t help it,\u201d said the prince. \u201cLavater would have said I\nlack the bump of paternity.\u201d\n\n\u201cDon\u2019t joke; I mean to have a serious talk with you. Do you know\nI am dissatisfied with your younger son? Between ourselves\u201d (and her\nface assumed its melancholy expression), \u201che was mentioned at Her\nMajesty\u2019s and you were pitied....\u201d\n\nThe prince answered nothing, but she looked at him significantly,\nawaiting a reply. He frowned.\n\n\u201cWhat would you have me do?\u201d he said at last. \u201cYou know I did all\na father could for their education, and they have both turned out fools.\nHippolyte is at least a quiet fool, but Anatole is an active one. That\nis the only difference between them.\u201d He said this smiling in a way\nmore natural and animated than usual, so that the wrinkles round\nhis mouth very clearly revealed something unexpectedly coarse and\nunpleasant.\n\n\u201cAnd why are children born to such men as you? If you were not a\nfather there would be nothing I could reproach you with,\u201d said Anna\nP\u00e1vlovna, looking up pensively.\n\n\u201cI am your faithful slave and to you alone I can confess that my\nchildren are the bane of my life. It is the cross I have to bear. That\nis how I explain it to myself. It can\u2019t be helped!\u201d\n\nHe said no more, but expressed his resignation to cruel fate by a\ngesture. Anna P\u00e1vlovna meditated.\n\n\u201cHave you never thought of marrying your prodigal son Anatole?\u201d she\nasked. \u201cThey say old maids have a mania for matchmaking, and though I\ndon\u2019t feel that weakness in myself as yet, I know a little person who\nis very unhappy with her father. She is a relation of yours, Princess\nMary Bolk\u00f3nskaya.\u201d\n\nPrince Vas\u00edli did not reply, though, with the quickness of memory and\nperception befitting a man of the world, he indicated by a movement of\nthe head that he was considering this information.\n\n\u201cDo you know,\u201d he said at last, evidently unable to check the sad\ncurrent of his thoughts, \u201cthat Anatole is costing me forty thousand\nrubles a year? And,\u201d he went on after a pause, \u201cwhat will it be in\nfive years, if he goes on like this?\u201d Presently he added: \u201cThat\u2019s\nwhat we fathers have to put up with.... Is this princess of yours\nrich?\u201d\n\n\u201cHer father is very rich and stingy. He lives in the country. He is\nthe well-known Prince Bolk\u00f3nski who had to retire from the army under\nthe late Emperor, and was nicknamed \u2018the King of Prussia.\u2019 He is\nvery clever but eccentric, and a bore. The poor girl is very unhappy.\nShe has a brother; I think you know him, he married Lise Meinen lately.\nHe is an aide-de-camp of Kut\u00fazov\u2019s and will be here tonight.\u201d\n\n\u201cListen, dear Annette,\u201d said the prince, suddenly taking Anna\nP\u00e1vlovna\u2019s hand and for some reason drawing it downwards. \u201cArrange\nthat affair for me and I shall always be your most devoted slave-slafe\nwith an f, as a village elder of mine writes in his reports. She is rich\nand of good family and that\u2019s all I want.\u201d\n\nAnd with the familiarity and easy grace peculiar to him, he raised the\nmaid of honor\u2019s hand to his lips, kissed it, and swung it to and fro\nas he lay back in his armchair, looking in another direction.\n\n\u201cAttendez,\u201d said Anna P\u00e1vlovna, reflecting, \u201cI\u2019ll speak to\nLise, young Bolk\u00f3nski\u2019s wife, this very evening, and perhaps the\nthing can be arranged. It shall be on your family\u2019s behalf that I\u2019ll\nstart my apprenticeship as old maid.\u201d\n\n\n\n\n\nCHAPTER II\n\nAnna P\u00e1vlovna\u2019s drawing room was gradually filling. The highest\nPetersburg society was assembled there: people differing widely in age\nand character but alike in the social circle to which they belonged.\nPrince Vas\u00edli\u2019s daughter, the beautiful H\u00e9l\u00e8ne, came to take her\nfather to the ambassador\u2019s entertainment; she wore a ball dress and\nher badge as maid of honor. The youthful little Princess Bolk\u00f3nskaya,\nknown as la femme la plus s\u00e9duisante de P\u00e9tersbourg, * was also there.\nShe had been married during the previous winter, and being pregnant did\nnot go to any large gatherings, but only to small receptions. Prince\nVas\u00edli\u2019s son, Hippolyte, had come with Mortemart, whom he introduced.\nThe Abb\u00e9 Morio and many others had also come.\n\n     * The most fascinating woman in Petersburg.\n\nTo each new arrival Anna P\u00e1vlovna said, \u201cYou have not yet seen my\naunt,\u201d or \u201cYou do not know my aunt?\u201d and very gravely conducted\nhim or her to a little old lady, wearing large bows of ribbon in her\ncap, who had come sailing in from another room as soon as the guests\nbegan to arrive; and slowly turning her eyes from the visitor to her\naunt, Anna P\u00e1vlovna mentioned each one\u2019s name and then left them.\n\nEach visitor performed the ceremony of greeting this old aunt whom not\none of them knew, not one of them wanted to know, and not one of them\ncared about; Anna P\u00e1vlovna observed these greetings with mournful and\nsolemn interest and silent approval. The aunt spoke to each of them in\nthe same words, about their health and her own, and the health of Her\nMajesty, \u201cwho, thank God, was better today.\u201d And each visitor,\nthough politeness prevented his showing impatience, left the old woman\nwith a sense of relief at having performed a vexatious duty and did not\nreturn to her the whole evening.\n\nThe young Princess Bolk\u00f3nskaya had brought some work in a\ngold-embroidered velvet bag. Her pretty little upper lip, on which a\ndelicate dark down was just perceptible, was too short for her teeth,\nbut it lifted all the more sweetly, and was especially charming when she\noccasionally drew it down to meet the lower lip. As is always the case\nwith a thoroughly attractive woman, her defect\u2014the shortness of her\nupper lip and her half-open mouth\u2014seemed to be her own special and\npeculiar form of beauty. Everyone brightened at the sight of this pretty\nyoung woman, so soon to become a mother, so full of life and health, and\ncarrying her burden so lightly. Old men and dull dispirited young ones\nwho looked at her, after being in her company and talking to her a\nlittle while, felt as if they too were becoming, like her, full of life\nand health. All who talked to her, and at each word saw her bright smile\nand the constant gleam of her white teeth, thought that they were in a\nspecially amiable mood that day.\n\nThe little princess went round the table with quick, short, swaying\nsteps, her workbag on her arm, and gaily spreading out her dress sat\ndown on a sofa near the silver samovar, as if all she was doing was a\npleasure to herself and to all around her. \u201cI have brought my work,\u201d\nsaid she in French, displaying her bag and addressing all present.\n\u201cMind, Annette, I hope you have not played a wicked trick on me,\u201d\nshe added, turning to her hostess. \u201cYou wrote that it was to be quite\na small reception, and just see how badly I am dressed.\u201d And she\nspread out her arms to show her short-waisted, lace-trimmed, dainty gray\ndress, girdled with a broad ribbon just below the breast.\n\n\u201cSoyez tranquille, Lise, you will always be prettier than anyone\nelse,\u201d replied Anna P\u00e1vlovna.\n\n\u201cYou know,\u201d said the princess in the same tone of voice and still in\nFrench, turning to a general, \u201cmy husband is deserting me? He is going\nto get himself killed. Tell me what this wretched war is for?\u201d she\nadded, addressing Prince Vas\u00edli, and without waiting for an answer she\nturned to speak to his daughter, the beautiful H\u00e9l\u00e8ne.\n\n\u201cWhat a delightful woman this little princess is!\u201d said Prince\nVas\u00edli to Anna P\u00e1vlovna.\n\nOne of the next arrivals was a stout, heavily built young man with\nclose-cropped hair, spectacles, the light-colored breeches fashionable\nat that time, a very high ruffle, and a brown dress coat. This stout\nyoung man was an illegitimate son of Count Bez\u00fakhov, a well-known\ngrandee of Catherine\u2019s time who now lay dying in Moscow. The young man\nhad not yet entered either the military or civil service, as he had only\njust returned from abroad where he had been educated, and this was his\nfirst appearance in society. Anna P\u00e1vlovna greeted him with the nod she\naccorded to the lowest hierarchy in her drawing room. But in spite of\nthis lowest-grade greeting, a look of anxiety and fear, as at the sight\nof something too large and unsuited to the place, came over her face\nwhen she saw Pierre enter.
